title: CRITICAL_PROCESS_DIED
summary: Stop code 0xEF appears when a process Windows depends on (for example csrss.exe, wininit.exe or services.exe) ends without warning. The crash tends to show up right after you sign in, or it repeats on every boot.
meaning: Windows treats a small set of processes as non-negotiable: the Client Server Runtime Subsystem, Session Manager, Windows Logon, services.exe and lsass.exe. If any of them is corrupted or exits, the kernel stops the PC on purpose, since carrying on could quietly damage your data. The stop parameters tell you which process was lost. These components start during boot, so once something breaks them the blue screen often comes back every time the PC starts.
commonCauses: Damaged system files, or a Windows Update that failed or was interrupted partway
A kernel-mode driver that is buggy or not compatible with your Windows build
Bad memory or disk corruption that damages the files these processes load from
Malware that targets core system processes or tries to hide inside them
Hardware that is failing or an overclock that is not stable

fixes.title: Reboot and review Event Viewer
fixes.detail: First, just restart the PC. If the blue screen does not come back, launch Event Viewer (`eventvwr.msc`), open Windows Logs > System, and find the critical event logged at the time of the crash. It usually tells you which process stopped.

fixes.title: Bring Windows and your drivers up to date
fixes.detail: Go to Settings > Windows Update and install whatever is waiting. Next, get current graphics, chipset and storage drivers directly from each manufacturer's website. A driver that was updated recently is one of the most common causes of this stop code.

fixes.title: Fix damaged system files using SFC and DISM
fixes.detail: Open Command Prompt as administrator. Run `sfc /scannow`, follow it with `DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth`, and then run `sfc /scannow` one more time. Restart when all three have finished.

fixes.title: Check the PC for malware
fixes.detail: Open Windows Security > Virus & threat protection > Scan options and run either a Full scan or a Microsoft Defender Offline scan. The offline scan restarts the PC and can catch threats that hide while Windows is running.

fixes.title: Check your memory with Windows Memory Diagnostic
fixes.detail: Run `mdsched.exe` and pick 'Restart now and check for problems (recommended)'. If a memory stick reports errors, replace it. If you want a more thorough test, let MemTest86 run overnight.
fixes.riskNote: The test runs before Windows loads, so expect the PC to be unavailable for at least 15-30 minutes.

fixes.title: Remove the latest update if the crashes continue
fixes.detail: If you can still get into Windows, go to Settings > Windows Update > Update history > Uninstall updates. You can also open an elevated prompt and run a command such as `wusa /uninstall /kb:4056892`, using the KB number listed in your own update history instead. If the PC is stuck in a boot loop, use the 'Uninstall Updates' option in Windows Recovery.

prevention: Install Windows and driver updates regularly, and never switch off the power while an update is running
When you add new RAM, test it with `mdsched.exe` before you push the PC hard
Leave System Restore turned on and keep your backups up to date
Hold off on overclocking until the PC has run reliably for a while
Check Event Viewer after any unexpected restart so you catch a failing component early

title: MEMORY_MANAGEMENT
summary: Stop code 0x1A means the Windows memory manager found its record of physical memory in a broken state. Bad RAM, an unstable overclock, or a driver that corrupts memory is behind it almost every time.
meaning: The memory manager keeps track of every physical page of RAM and maintains the page tables. A 0x1A crash tells you it found a page in a condition that should never happen, such as a page released twice or one assigned to the wrong owner. Windows stops right away so the damage cannot spread unnoticed into your files. Most of the time the cause is faulty RAM or a kernel-mode driver writing into memory that belongs to something else.
commonCauses: RAM modules that are defective, mismatched or not fully seated
A kernel-mode driver with a bug that overwrites memory
Aggressive XMP memory profiles or an overclock that is not stable
Corruption on the disk that affects the page file
Malware, or other hardware that is starting to fail

fixes.title: Test memory with Windows Memory Diagnostic
fixes.detail: Launch `mdsched.exe`, pick 'Restart now and check for problems (recommended)', and let the whole test run. For a more definitive answer, follow up with several passes of MemTest86.
fixes.riskNote: The diagnostic runs before Windows loads, so set aside time when you do not need the PC.

fixes.title: Turn off overclocking and XMP profiles
fixes.detail: Open BIOS/UEFI setup (usually by pressing F2 or Del during startup) and load the default settings, or disable XMP/EXPO along with any CPU or memory overclock. Then see whether the PC stays stable at stock speeds.

fixes.title: Reseat the RAM and test one stick at a time
fixes.detail: Shut down and unplug the PC. Remove each memory stick and press it firmly back into its slot. Then boot with a single stick installed to find out which module is bad, and try each slot too, since a slot can fail as well.
fixes.riskNote: Unplug the power cord, and touch bare metal on the case first to discharge static.

fixes.title: Install Windows and driver updates
fixes.detail: Install any pending Windows updates, then get new graphics, chipset and storage drivers from the manufacturers' websites. Old drivers that corrupt memory are a frequent cause of this crash.

fixes.title: Fix system files and scan the disk
fixes.detail: Run `sfc /scannow` first, then `DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth`. Finish with `chkdsk C: /f /r`, which checks the drive, including the area where the page file lives.
fixes.riskNote: On a large drive, `chkdsk /r` can run for hours. Back up anything important before you start.

prevention: Buy RAM as a matched kit, and avoid combining modules of different speeds or brands
Run the memory diagnostic every time you install new RAM
Keep your BIOS, chipset drivers and GPU drivers up to date
Leave XMP and overclocking off until the PC has proven stable under heavy load

title: IRQL_NOT_LESS_OR_EQUAL
summary: Stop code 0xA appears when a driver or other kernel-mode code reads memory it should not access at its current interrupt request level. A buggy driver is the usual cause, and the blue screen often names the file responsible.
meaning: Every operation in kernel mode runs at an Interrupt Request Level (IRQL). At the higher levels, code may only touch memory that is guaranteed to stay in RAM and never get paged out. A 0xA crash means a driver or kernel component tried to use a bad address while running at too high a level. The stop screen usually lists a file name, often a .sys driver, and that name is your best lead for fixing the problem.
commonCauses: An outdated or buggy kernel-mode driver, often for network, audio or graphics hardware
Bad RAM that returns corrupted data
Antivirus, VPN or firewall software that installs kernel filter drivers
An overclock that is not stable
Damaged system files

fixes.title: Write down the driver file shown on the blue screen
fixes.detail: The stop screen normally lists a module, for example a .sys file. Search for that exact file name to find out which device and vendor it belongs to. The fix almost always involves that driver.

fixes.title: Update the named driver, or roll it back
fixes.detail: Get the newest driver from the device manufacturer. If the crashes started right after a driver update, open Device Manager and choose 'Roll back driver' for that device instead.

fixes.title: Remove security or VPN software you installed recently
fixes.detail: Third-party antivirus, VPN and firewall products add kernel filters, and those filters often trigger this stop code. Uninstall the most recent one, restart, and see if the crashes stop.

fixes.title: Repair Windows with SFC and DISM
fixes.detail: To rule out damaged system files, open an elevated prompt and run `sfc /scannow`, then `DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth`, and then `sfc /scannow` once more.

fixes.title: Check RAM and undo any overclock
fixes.detail: Run `mdsched.exe` to test memory. Load the BIOS defaults as well, which turns off XMP and any overclock settings.

fixes.title: Find the bad driver with Driver Verifier
fixes.detail: From an elevated prompt, run `verifier`, choose the standard settings, and select all third-party drivers. Use the PC until the crash happens again. The new blue screen will name the driver at fault.
fixes.riskNote: Driver Verifier crashes Windows on purpose when it catches a misbehaving driver, and it can leave you in a boot loop. Make sure you know how to get into Safe Mode, where `verifier /reset` turns it off.

prevention: Get drivers from the device manufacturer instead of old discs that came in the box
As soon as crashes begin, roll back or remove the newest driver before the problem repeats
Run only one real-time security product at a time
Avoid tuning an overclock at the same time you install new drivers

title: PAGE_FAULT_IN_NONPAGED_AREA
summary: Stop code 0x50 happens when a process or driver points to memory that is supposed to stay in physical RAM at all times, and that memory turns out to be missing or invalid. The usual suspects are bad RAM, a faulty driver, or disk corruption.
meaning: Non-paged memory is kernel memory that Windows never moves out to disk, because it is used at interrupt level where paging cannot happen. A 0x50 crash means something tried to use a page in that pool that was not valid. The problem involves both memory and storage, so causes are split fairly evenly between bad RAM, buggy drivers, and corruption in NTFS or the page file. Antivirus filter drivers also show up often.
commonCauses: Faulty RAM, or RAM pushed past its rated speed
A kernel-mode driver with a bug
Disk errors that corrupt the NTFS volume or the page file
Filter drivers installed by antivirus or other security software
Damaged system files

fixes.title: Test memory with Windows Memory Diagnostic
fixes.detail: Launch `mdsched.exe`, pick the restart-and-check option, and let it run to the end. Replace any memory stick that reports errors.

fixes.title: Scan the drive with chkdsk
fixes.detail: Open an elevated prompt, run `chkdsk C: /f /r`, and agree to run the scan at the next restart. It fixes file system errors and marks bad sectors that could otherwise corrupt the page file.
fixes.riskNote: If the drive already shows signs of failing, copy your important data off it before you run chkdsk.

fixes.title: Repair Windows with SFC and DISM
fixes.detail: Run `sfc /scannow`, then `DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth`, then `sfc /scannow` a second time, and restart.

fixes.title: Update drivers, or roll back a recent one
fixes.detail: Get the latest storage, network and graphics drivers from the manufacturers. If the crashes began after a driver update, open Device Manager and roll that driver back.

fixes.title: Remove third-party antivirus for now
fixes.detail: Fully uninstall your third-party security suite (disabling it is not enough) so its kernel filter driver is out of the picture. Let Microsoft Defender protect the PC while you test.

prevention: Run the memory diagnostic any time you install new RAM
Keep Windows and your drivers current, using the manufacturers' own downloads
Replace aging drives as soon as SMART warnings appear
Leave 15-20% of the system drive free

title: KERNEL_SECURITY_CHECK_FAILURE
summary: Stop code 0x139 means the kernel ran a fail-fast security check, found a critical data structure that had been changed or corrupted, and halted right away. A driver handing over bad data, faulty RAM, or malware is usually to blame.
meaning: Current versions of Windows protect sensitive kernel data with integrity checks such as stack cookies and structure validation. If one of those checks fails, the kernel 'fails fast' with stop 0x139 instead of continuing with data it can no longer trust. The check itself is dependable, so the crash points to whatever fed it the corrupted data: a faulty driver, memory corruption, malware, or damaged system files.
commonCauses: An outdated or buggy driver, commonly for graphics, network or storage hardware
Bad RAM or an overclock that is not stable
System files damaged by an update that failed
Malware tampering with kernel data
Software installed recently that includes kernel components

fixes.title: Install Windows updates and current third-party drivers
fixes.detail: Install any updates Windows is waiting on, and get fresh GPU, network and chipset drivers from the manufacturers. If the crashes started after a driver update, roll that driver back instead.

fixes.title: Repair Windows with SFC and DISM
fixes.detail: Run `sfc /scannow`, then `DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth`, then `sfc /scannow` again. Restart when you are done.

fixes.title: Check the RAM
fixes.detail: Use `mdsched.exe` to run a complete Windows Memory Diagnostic pass. Turn off XMP and any overclock in the BIOS while you test.

fixes.title: Check the PC for malware
fixes.detail: Open Windows Security > Virus & threat protection > Scan options and run a Full scan or a Microsoft Defender Offline scan.

fixes.title: Remove software you installed recently
fixes.detail: Uninstall or update any security, VPN or virtualization software added shortly before the crashes started. Restart and see whether the problem continues.

fixes.title: Track down the driver with Driver Verifier
fixes.detail: Run `verifier`, use the standard settings, and select the third-party drivers. Use the PC until it crashes again, then uninstall the driver it flags. Run `verifier /reset` to turn Verifier off afterward.
fixes.riskNote: Verifier crashes the PC the moment it catches a faulty driver, which can lead to a boot loop. Make sure you can get into Safe Mode before you start.

prevention: Install Windows and driver updates on a regular schedule
Test any new RAM, and leave the BIOS on default settings until the PC is stable
Scan the PC whenever you suspect an infection
Stay away from beta or preview drivers on a computer you rely on

title: SYSTEM_SERVICE_EXCEPTION
summary: Stop code 0x3B means Windows hit an exception while running a system service routine. It is closely linked to graphics drivers, antivirus filter drivers and damaged system files.
meaning: When an app asks Windows for a system service, the call crosses into kernel code, and that code has to finish without errors. A 0x3B crash means an unexpected exception happened during that handoff. In practice the causes tend to be graphics drivers (several well-known GPU driver bugs produce exactly this code), security software that adds kernel filters, and damaged system files.
commonCauses: A graphics driver that is outdated or has a bug
Antivirus or other security software running kernel filter drivers
Damage to system files or the component store
Bad RAM
Software installed recently that includes kernel components

fixes.title: Update or reinstall the graphics driver
fixes.detail: In Device Manager, uninstall the GPU driver, checking 'Delete the driver software' if that option appears. Restart, then install the newest driver from NVIDIA, AMD or Intel.

fixes.title: Repair Windows with SFC and DISM
fixes.detail: Run `sfc /scannow`, then `DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth`, then `sfc /scannow` again. Restart when you are done.

fixes.title: Update or reinstall your antivirus
fixes.detail: Update your third-party security suite to its newest version, or uninstall it for now so you can test. Turn on Microsoft Defender to protect the PC while it is removed.
fixes.riskNote: Do not leave the PC without protection. Reinstall your antivirus or switch Defender on as soon as you finish testing.

fixes.title: Check the RAM
fixes.detail: Run `mdsched.exe` and let Windows Memory Diagnostic finish. Turn off overclocking and XMP while you test.

fixes.title: Remove software you installed recently
fixes.detail: Uninstall any software that runs at kernel level (security tools, virtualization apps, RGB or system utilities) that you added just before the crashes began. Then see whether the crashes continue.

fixes.title: Install any waiting Windows updates
fixes.detail: Microsoft has included fixes for this stop code in past cumulative updates. Go to Settings > Windows Update > Check for updates, install what is offered, and restart.

prevention: Get GPU drivers from the manufacturer instead of depending only on Windows Update
Keep your security software current, or use the built-in Microsoft Defender
Run SFC and DISM after any failed update or hard crash
Avoid beta kernel-level software on the computer you use every day

title: DPC_WATCHDOG_VIOLATION
summary: Stop code 0x133 means a deferred procedure call (DPC) ran too long, or a device did not respond before its timeout. Common causes are an incompatible storage driver, outdated SSD firmware, or buggy graphics or network drivers.
meaning: Drivers queue up DPCs, which are high-priority kernel tasks that have to finish fast so the scheduler can keep running. A watchdog times them. If a DPC runs past its limit, or a device never reports that its work is done, Windows stops with 0x133. Microsoft's documentation links this code to incompatible SSD and AHCI drivers, most famously the old iastor driver after a Windows 10 upgrade. Most other cases come from graphics, network and other peripheral drivers.
commonCauses: Storage or AHCI drivers that are not compatible, or old SSD firmware
Graphics, network or chipset drivers with bugs
A peripheral that was just connected or is failing
System files damaged during an upgrade
An SSD or hard drive that is starting to fail

fixes.title: Update the storage controller driver
fixes.detail: Open Device Manager, expand 'IDE ATA/ATAPI controllers', and update the AHCI or RAID controller driver. If the PC uses a legacy iastor driver, change the controller to Microsoft's 'Standard SATA AHCI Controller' driver. That swap is the documented workaround for this stop code after an upgrade.
fixes.riskNote: Create a restore point before you start. The wrong storage driver can stop Windows from booting.

fixes.title: Update SSD firmware plus graphics and network drivers
fixes.detail: Use the SSD maker's toolbox app to install the latest firmware. Then get current graphics and network drivers from the manufacturers' websites.

fixes.title: Unplug USB devices you do not need
fixes.detail: Disconnect external drives, docks and adapters, then restart. One misbehaving device that holds up a DPC is enough to cause this exact stop code.

fixes.title: Repair Windows with SFC and DISM
fixes.detail: Run `sfc /scannow`, then `DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth`, and finish with `sfc /scannow` again.

fixes.title: Check drive health
fixes.detail: In Event Viewer, look under Windows Logs > System for disk errors from the 'disk' or 'stornvme' source, and run the SSD manufacturer's health utility. Replace any drive that reports reallocated sectors or timeouts.

prevention: Reinstall chipset and storage drivers after each Windows feature update
Use the manufacturer's tool to keep SSD firmware up to date
Do not connect storage devices through cheap USB adapters or hubs
Watch drive health readings and replace aging SSDs before they fail

title: UNEXPECTED_STORE_EXCEPTION
summary: Stop code 0x154 means the 'store manager', the kernel component that caches and compresses app memory, hit an exception it could not deal with. Typical causes include disk or page file trouble, Fast Startup, antivirus software and storage drivers.
meaning: The name is misleading: this crash has nothing to do with the Microsoft Store. The 'store' here is the part of memory management that handles compressed memory pages for apps. When it fails, something underneath it is usually at fault: a drive struggling to keep up with page file reads and writes, a filter driver corrupting I/O, or Fast Startup bringing back a session that was already broken. It often happens while the PC is sitting idle.
commonCauses: Disk errors or a failing drive that affect the page file
Fast Startup restoring a session that was already corrupted
Filter drivers from antivirus or storage software
Storage controller drivers with bugs
Bad RAM

fixes.title: Scan the drive with chkdsk
fixes.detail: Open an elevated prompt, run `chkdsk C: /f /r`, and let the scan run when the PC restarts. This is the fix that resolves this stop code most often.
fixes.riskNote: If the drive shows any other signs of failing, back up important data before you start.

fixes.title: Turn off Fast Startup
fixes.detail: Open Control Panel > Power Options > 'Choose what the power buttons do', click 'Change settings that are currently unavailable', and clear 'Turn on fast startup'. Shut the PC down completely, then turn it back on.

fixes.title: Repair Windows with SFC and DISM
fixes.detail: Run `sfc /scannow`, then `DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth`, then `sfc /scannow` again. Restart when you are done.

fixes.title: Update storage and graphics drivers
fixes.detail: Get current chipset, storage and GPU drivers from the manufacturers' websites, and use the SSD maker's tool to update the drive's firmware.

fixes.title: Check the RAM
fixes.detail: Use `mdsched.exe` for a complete memory test, with XMP and overclocking turned off while it runs.

prevention: Replace drives that log disk errors in Event Viewer
Turn off Fast Startup on PCs that act strangely after sleep or idle time
Keep SSD firmware and storage drivers up to date
Run SFC and DISM health checks from time to time

title: KERNEL_DATA_INPAGE_ERROR
summary: Stop code 0x7A means Windows tried to read a page of kernel data back from the paging file and failed. A drive with bad sectors, a cable problem, faulty RAM, or a corrupted page file is usually responsible.
meaning: When RAM gets tight, Windows writes kernel data out to disk and reads it back when it is needed again. A 0x7A crash means one of those reads did not work, so the data never made it back into memory. The first stop parameter often contains an NTSTATUS code, such as 0xC000009C or 0xC0000185, that points to a device I/O or media error. Take this stop code seriously as an early warning about your drive's health.
commonCauses: A drive that is failing, with bad sectors or controller errors
Bad RAM that corrupts data while it is being read
SATA data or power cables that are loose or damaged
A page file that was corrupted because its volume is damaged
Malware, or I/O errors caused by a driver

fixes.title: Scan the drive with chkdsk
fixes.detail: Open an elevated prompt, run `chkdsk C: /f /r`, and let the offline scan run at restart. It repairs file system damage and marks bad sectors so Windows stops using them.
fixes.riskNote: Back up important data before you run chkdsk. Repeated inpage errors are often an early warning that the drive is about to fail.

fixes.title: Look at the drive's health
fixes.detail: For a quick pass or fail answer, run `wmic diskdrive get status`. Then look in Event Viewer (System log, source 'disk') and run the drive maker's SMART utility. Replace the drive if it reports reallocated or pending sectors.

fixes.title: Check the RAM
fixes.detail: Run `mdsched.exe`. Faulty memory can corrupt data while it is being paged and trigger this same stop code.

fixes.title: Inspect the data and power cables
fixes.detail: On a desktop, shut down and firmly reconnect the SATA data and power cables at both the drive and the motherboard, or reseat the M.2 drive. If that does not help, try a different cable.

fixes.title: Repair with SFC and DISM, then scan for malware
fixes.detail: Fix system files with `sfc /scannow` and `DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth`. Then run a full Microsoft Defender scan.

prevention: Keep an eye on SMART health data and replace any drive that raises warnings
Keep your backups current, since this stop code often comes before a drive fails
Use good-quality cables and make sure connectors inside the case are seated securely
Test your memory whenever files get corrupted for no obvious reason

title: BAD_SYSTEM_CONFIG_INFO
summary: Stop code 0x74 means Windows could not load a valid system configuration because the SYSTEM registry hive or the boot configuration is corrupted or does not match. Normally the PC crashes in a loop and cannot start.
meaning: During startup, the kernel reads the SYSTEM registry hive to find out which devices, services and drivers to load. A 0x74 crash means that information is damaged or no longer matches what the kernel expects. This usually happens after a failed update, disk corruption, hand edits to the registry, or a hardware change. Windows needs that data to boot, so normal startup keeps failing, and you have to make repairs from Windows RE (the recovery environment).
commonCauses: A Windows Update that failed or was cut short and corrupted the SYSTEM hive
Corruption on the system drive
Registry edits made by hand or by third-party 'cleaner' tools
A hardware change that clashes with the saved configuration
Damaged boot configuration data (BCD)

fixes.title: Get into Windows Recovery (WinRE)
fixes.detail: Interrupt startup three times in a row (turn the power off while the dots are spinning) and Windows will open the recovery environment. You can also boot from Windows installation media and choose 'Repair your computer'.

fixes.title: Run Startup Repair
fixes.detail: In WinRE, go to Troubleshoot > Advanced options > Startup Repair and let it try to fix the boot configuration automatically.

fixes.title: Remove the latest quality update from WinRE
fixes.detail: Go to Troubleshoot > Advanced options > Uninstall Updates and choose 'Uninstall latest quality update'. This is the usual fix when an update broke the configuration.

fixes.title: Roll back with System Restore from WinRE
fixes.detail: Choose Troubleshoot > Advanced options > System Restore and pick a restore point from before the first crash. Your personal files are not changed by System Restore.

fixes.title: Rebuild the boot files from the WinRE command prompt
fixes.detail: Open Advanced options > Command Prompt and run `bootrec /fixmbr`, `bootrec /fixboot` and `bootrec /rebuildbcd`. Then run `chkdsk C: /f /r` to check for disk corruption.
fixes.riskNote: Check which drive letter Windows has inside WinRE before rebuilding anything. It is not always C:.

prevention: Never cut the power during an update. Let the 'working on updates' screen finish on its own
Avoid registry cleaners and so-called 'optimizer' tools
Leave System Restore on, and create a restore point before any big change
Back up regularly so that repairing Windows is not a big deal

title: INACCESSIBLE_BOOT_DEVICE
summary: Stop code 0x7B means Windows lost contact with the system drive during startup and cannot keep booting. Typical causes are a storage driver mismatch, a change to the BIOS SATA mode, a failing drive, or a bad update.
meaning: Early in startup, the firmware hands control to the Windows storage drivers, which then have to find the system partition. A 0x7B crash means that handoff did not work. The correct storage driver might be missing or wrong, the controller mode might have changed (AHCI, RAID or IDE), the boot files might point to the wrong device, or the drive itself might not be responding. Windows then restarts over and over, and only the recovery environment is available.
commonCauses: A Windows Update or feature upgrade that left out the right storage driver
A BIOS reset, or a change to the SATA or NVMe mode (AHCI versus RAID or IDE)
A system drive that is failing or has come disconnected
Damaged boot configuration data (BCD)
A cloned or migrated system that points to the wrong boot device

fixes.title: Get into Windows Recovery (WinRE)
fixes.detail: Interrupt startup three times to make Windows launch automatic repair, or boot from Windows installation media and choose 'Repair your computer'.

fixes.title: Run Startup Repair and remove the latest update
fixes.detail: In WinRE, run Troubleshoot > Advanced options > Startup Repair. If the problem began after an update, go to 'Uninstall Updates' and choose 'Uninstall latest quality update'.

fixes.title: Check the BIOS SATA or storage mode
fixes.detail: Open BIOS/UEFI setup and check that the SATA mode (AHCI or RAID/IDE) is the same one Windows was installed with. If the mode was recently changed or the BIOS was reset, change it back. Switching modes without preparing Windows first leaves it unable to boot.
fixes.riskNote: Switching between AHCI and RAID by trial and error can make things worse. Go back to the previous setting first.

fixes.title: Unplug extra drives and USB devices
fixes.detail: Shut down, disconnect any drives, USB sticks and external disks you do not need, and try again. A shuffled drive order can confuse the boot process.

fixes.title: Rebuild the boot files and scan the drive
fixes.detail: In the WinRE Command Prompt, run `bootrec /fixmbr`, `bootrec /fixboot` and `bootrec /rebuildbcd`, followed by `chkdsk C: /f /r`. If SMART data shows the drive is failing, replace it.

prevention: Reinstall chipset and storage drivers after each feature upgrade
Never change the BIOS SATA mode without preparing Windows first (the msconfig method for a safe AHCI switch)
Keep a recent backup image of the system drive
Update the BIOS and firmware before a major Windows upgrade instead of after it

title: WHEA_UNCORRECTABLE_ERROR
summary: Stop code 0x124 (WHEA) means the processor or platform reported a serious hardware error that Windows could not correct. It is the classic sign of an unstable overclock, overheating, failing hardware, or an out-of-date BIOS.
meaning: WHEA, short for Windows Hardware Error Architecture, gathers machine-check and platform errors that the CPU and chipset report. A 0x124 crash happens when one of those errors is marked 'uncorrectable': a cache, bus, memory or processor fault serious enough that it is no longer safe to keep running. Event Viewer records the failing component in 'WHEA-Logger' entries, so check those first.
commonCauses: An unstable CPU or RAM overclock, or an aggressive XMP/EXPO profile
The CPU, GPU or voltage regulator (VRM) running too hot
A CPU, motherboard, power supply or RAM module that is failing
Old BIOS/UEFI or chipset firmware
A power supply that is too small or wearing out

fixes.title: Turn off overclocking and XMP/EXPO
fixes.detail: Open BIOS/UEFI and load the optimized defaults. If you overclock, go back to stock speeds and voltages, and confirm the PC is stable before you turn any profile back on.

fixes.title: Update the BIOS/UEFI and chipset drivers
fixes.detail: Install the newest BIOS from the motherboard manufacturer along with current chipset drivers. Firmware releases often include fixes for WHEA problems.
fixes.riskNote: A BIOS update that fails partway can brick the motherboard. Follow the manufacturer's instructions exactly and make sure the power will not be interrupted.

fixes.title: Check temperatures and cooling
fixes.detail: Check CPU and GPU temperatures with the BIOS hardware monitor or the manufacturer's tool. If they run hot under load, clean out the dust, make sure every fan is turning, and reseat the CPU cooler.

fixes.title: Check the RAM
fixes.detail: Run `mdsched.exe`, or let MemTest86 run several passes, with XMP turned off. Replace any module that fails.

fixes.title: Read the WHEA-Logger events and reseat hardware
fixes.detail: In Event Viewer, filter the System log by 'WHEA-Logger' to see which component reported the error (for example a corrected or uncorrected cache or bus error). Then reseat the RAM, the GPU and the power connectors. If errors keep coming, suspect the power supply.

prevention: Prove any overclock with long stress tests before you use it every day
Keep the BIOS and chipset firmware up to date
Look after your cooling by cleaning dust filters and fans regularly
Choose a good-quality power supply with room to spare above your system's peak draw

title: CLOCK_WATCHDOG_TIMEOUT
summary: Stop code 0x101 means one of the secondary CPU cores did not respond in time, so it looked frozen. Common causes are an unstable overclock, BIOS bugs, power delivery problems, or a driver that holds a lock for too long.
meaning: On a multi-core processor, each core has to handle its clock interrupt on time. The clock watchdog checks that this happens. A 0x101 crash means a core did not check in within the expected window, so the kernel treats it as stuck. In practice, causes fall into two groups: hardware or platform instability (overclocking, voltage, heat, BIOS) and software that hogs a core, such as a driver spinning on a lock.
commonCauses: An unstable CPU overclock or undervolt
BIOS/UEFI firmware that is old or has bugs
Overheating, or a power supply that cannot deliver enough power
A driver holding a spinlock so long that a core gets no other work done
A borderline CPU or motherboard

fixes.title: Load BIOS defaults and remove overclocks
fixes.detail: Load the optimized defaults in BIOS/UEFI, turn off XMP/EXPO, undo any CPU voltage changes, and test at stock settings. Most 0x101 crashes come down to instability.

fixes.title: Update the BIOS/UEFI
fixes.detail: Install the newest BIOS for your motherboard. Manufacturers release fixes aimed at clock watchdog and core-hang problems. Follow their update instructions carefully.
fixes.riskNote: If a BIOS update is interrupted, the motherboard can be bricked. Do it on reliable power.

fixes.title: Update chipset and graphics drivers
fixes.detail: Get current chipset and graphics drivers from the manufacturers' websites to rule out a driver that is tying up a core.

fixes.title: Check cooling and power delivery
fixes.detail: Check CPU temperatures under load, and make sure every power connector is fully seated, including the extra CPU EPS cables. If you have a power supply you know works, try it.

fixes.title: Check the RAM
fixes.detail: Run `mdsched.exe` or MemTest86. Memory errors at the memory controller level can stall a core and cause this stop code.

prevention: Stress-test any overclock for hours, not minutes, before you trust it
Keep the BIOS, CPU microcode and chipset drivers up to date
Keep the CPU properly cooled and make sure air moves freely through the case
Do not undervolt past the point you have tested as stable

title: VIDEO_SCHEDULER_INTERNAL_ERROR
summary: Stop code 0x119 means the DirectX video scheduler found a fatal problem inside the graphics stack, because the display driver failed one of its internal consistency checks. A GPU driver bug, a failing GPU or VRAM, or overclocking is the likely cause.
meaning: The video scheduler is the DirectX graphics kernel component that puts the GPU's work in order. A 0x119 crash means the scheduler saw the driver stack break its own rules and end up in a state it could not recover from. The first stop parameter identifies the specific violation. The most common causes are the GPU driver, faults in the GPU's memory (VRAM), and unstable GPU overclocks.
commonCauses: A GPU driver that has a bug or is corrupted
A GPU or its video memory (VRAM) failing
An unstable overclock on the GPU core or memory
The GPU overheating
Damaged system files in the graphics stack

fixes.title: Do a clean reinstall of the GPU driver
fixes.detail: In Device Manager, uninstall the display adapter and check 'delete the driver software'. Restart into Safe Mode, then install the newest driver from NVIDIA, AMD or Intel. A clean install replaces any corrupted driver files.

fixes.title: Remove any GPU overclock
fixes.detail: Use the GPU maker's tool to undo any core or memory overclock or factory OC profile (on cards with a dual BIOS, switch to the stock BIOS). Then test at stock settings.

fixes.title: Check GPU temperatures and power
fixes.detail: Watch the GPU temperature under load, clear dust out of the fans and heatsinks, and make sure the PCIe power connectors are pushed all the way in.

fixes.title: Repair Windows with SFC and DISM
fixes.detail: To repair the graphics stack files, run `sfc /scannow`, then `DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth`, then `sfc /scannow` again.

fixes.title: Test the graphics card hardware
fixes.detail: If the crashes continue with a clean driver at stock speeds, try the card in another PC or try a different card in this one. That shows whether the problem is the driver or failing hardware.

prevention: Get GPU drivers from the manufacturer and do not stack one driver install on top of another
Prove any GPU overclock with long stress tests
Keep the graphics card cool and free of dust
Replace the card if VRAM errors keep coming back

title: VIDEO_TDR_FAILURE
summary: Stop code 0x116 means the GPU driver stopped responding and Windows' timeout detection and recovery (TDR) could not reset it. Usually the GPU driver has a bug or the graphics hardware is failing, and the blue screen normally names the driver file.
meaning: If the display driver stops responding for more than about 2 seconds, Windows TDR tries to reset it without restarting the PC. A 0x116 crash means that reset did not work, so Windows had to stop. The blue screen usually lists the module, which tells you whose driver needs reinstalling: nvlddmkm.sys for NVIDIA, atikmdag.sys or amdkmdag.sys for AMD, and igdkmd64.sys for Intel. The problem stays within the graphics stack, so the PC generally boots normally afterward.
commonCauses: A GPU driver that has a bug or is corrupted
A failing GPU or failing VRAM
An unstable GPU overclock
The GPU running too hot under load
Driver conflicts after a Windows upgrade

fixes.title: Do a clean reinstall of the graphics driver
fixes.detail: In Device Manager, uninstall the display adapter and restart. Then install the newest driver for the module named on the blue screen (NVIDIA, AMD or Intel).

fixes.title: Roll the driver back if the crashes are new
fixes.detail: If the crashes started right after a driver update, open Device Manager, right-click the display adapter, choose Properties > Driver, and click 'Roll Back Driver'.

fixes.title: Turn off GPU overclocking
fixes.detail: Remove any core or memory overclock or factory performance profile, and test at stock settings before you turn a proven profile back on.

fixes.title: Check GPU temperatures and power connectors
fixes.detail: Watch temperatures under load, clean the cooler and fans, and reconnect the PCIe power cables firmly.

fixes.title: Repair Windows with SFC and DISM
fixes.detail: Run `sfc /scannow`, then `DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth`, and then run `sfc /scannow` a second time.

prevention: Always do a clean install when you put on GPU drivers from the manufacturer
Stress-test overclocks and undo any profile that is not stable
Keep the GPU cooler clean and make sure nothing blocks the airflow
If TDR failures keep happening even after clean driver installs, replace the GPU

title: DRIVER_IRQL_NOT_LESS_OR_EQUAL
summary: Stop code 0xD1 appears when a driver reaches for pageable or invalid memory while running at an interrupt level that forbids paging. A third-party driver is nearly always responsible, and the blue screen usually tells you which file it was.
meaning: Think of this as the driver-focused cousin of IRQL_NOT_LESS_OR_EQUAL. While operating at an elevated IRQL, a kernel-mode driver read or wrote an address that was either paged out or simply invalid, and Windows had to stop. The usual suspects are filter drivers from VPN and antivirus products, along with network, Wi-Fi and audio drivers. Look at the stop screen for the failing module (typically a .sys file): once you update or remove that driver, the crashes generally stop.
commonCauses: A defective driver for Wi-Fi, networking, audio or graphics
Kernel filter drivers installed by VPN clients or antivirus suites
A driver that has fallen out of date following a Windows feature update
Defective memory modules
Utility software that came with a recently connected peripheral

fixes.title: Find out which driver the blue screen blames
fixes.detail: Write down the module name shown on the stop screen (nvlddmkm.sys and netwtw10.sys are typical examples), then look it up to learn which device and manufacturer it belongs to. Every later step focuses on that driver.

fixes.title: Update the driver, or roll it back
fixes.detail: If the crashes began right after a driver update, open Device Manager and choose 'Roll back driver'. Otherwise, grab the newest release from the manufacturer's website. Removing the device and reinstalling its driver is another valid route.

fixes.title: Uninstall VPN and antivirus filter software
fixes.detail: Kernel filters from these products are among the most common triggers for 0xD1. If you added a third-party VPN client or security suite shortly before the crashes started, remove it and test again.

fixes.title: Repair system files with SFC and DISM
fixes.detail: From an elevated prompt, run `sfc /scannow` first, follow it with `DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth`, and then run `sfc /scannow` one more time.

fixes.title: Check memory and turn on Driver Verifier
fixes.detail: Use `mdsched.exe` to rule out bad RAM. If you still cannot pin down the culprit, launch `verifier`, pick the standard settings and target the third-party drivers so the faulty one is exposed.
fixes.riskNote: While Driver Verifier searches for the bad driver, the PC may get stuck in a boot loop. Boot into Safe Mode and run `verifier /reset` to turn it off.

prevention: Get network and audio drivers straight from the hardware manufacturer
Install driver updates one by one so a problem driver stands out right away
Keep VPN and antivirus software to a minimum and keep what you use up to date
Create a restore point before you test new hardware

title: KMODE_EXCEPTION_NOT_HANDLED
summary: Stop code 0x1E means code running in kernel mode threw an exception and no handler caught it. Typical culprits are a faulty driver, damaged system files, bad RAM or malware, and the stop screen may name the module involved.
meaning: Kernel components are supposed to deal with their own exceptions. When an exception goes unclaimed, Windows has no way to confirm the system is still in a safe state, so it halts with stop 0x1E. The stop parameters contain the exception code and frequently the address of the module that caused it. Most cases trace back to driver bugs, while corrupted system files and memory faults account for much of the rest.
commonCauses: A kernel-mode driver that is buggy or incompatible
System files damaged by an update that did not finish
Defective memory
Malware operating at the kernel level
Newly installed programs that include kernel components

fixes.title: Record any file name the blue screen displays
fixes.detail: When the stop screen shows a module name (frequently a .sys file), look it up to find which device owns it, and start by updating or rolling back that driver.

fixes.title: Repair system files with SFC and DISM
fixes.detail: In an elevated prompt, run `sfc /scannow`, then `DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth`, then `sfc /scannow` a second time. Restart once all three finish.

fixes.title: Remove software you installed recently
fixes.detail: Uninstall any security, virtualization or system utility programs that arrived just before the crashes began. Test after each removal so you can tell which one mattered.

fixes.title: Check your RAM
fixes.detail: Launch `mdsched.exe` and allow Windows Memory Diagnostic to run to completion. Turn off XMP and any overclocking for the duration of the test.

fixes.title: Scan the PC for malware
fixes.detail: Run a full scan in Microsoft Defender, or use Defender Offline, to eliminate kernel-level malware as a cause.

fixes.title: Apply any pending Windows updates
fixes.detail: Go to Settings > Windows Update and install everything available. Cumulative updates often carry compatibility fixes for older drivers.

prevention: Install drivers from the manufacturer, not from bundled driver packs
Make a restore point before adding software that runs in the kernel
Stay current on Windows updates
Scan downloaded files and schedule regular Defender scans

title: SYSTEM_THREAD_EXCEPTION_NOT_HANDLED
summary: Stop code 0x7E (or 0x1000007E) means a system thread threw an exception that nothing handled. The classic cause is a display driver such as atikmdag.sys or nvlddmkm.sys, though audio and network drivers do it too, often just after being updated.
meaning: System threads are worker threads inside the kernel, and they are not allowed to fail without warning. Stop 0x7E signals that one of them raised an exception with no handler to catch it. The 0x1000007E variant is the same error with an extra flag bit set. In most cases the blue screen names the module responsible, and graphics drivers top the list by a wide margin. That is why a fresh GPU driver install is the usual starting point.
commonCauses: A faulty graphics or display driver
An audio, network or other device driver that misbehaves after an update
Damaged system files
Defective memory
Filter drivers installed by antivirus software

fixes.title: Find the driver file shown on the blue screen
fixes.detail: Take the module name from the stop screen. For example, atikmdag.sys belongs to AMD graphics and nvlddmkm.sys to NVIDIA, while other names point to audio or network adapters. The remaining steps focus on that driver.

fixes.title: Do a clean reinstall of that driver
fixes.detail: In Device Manager, uninstall the device (for display adapters, tick 'delete the driver software'), restart, and then install the newest driver from the manufacturer. For graphics drivers, this fixes the majority of cases.

fixes.title: Repair system files with SFC and DISM
fixes.detail: From an elevated prompt, run `sfc /scannow`, follow with `DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth`, run `sfc /scannow` again, and restart.

fixes.title: Test the memory
fixes.detail: Run a complete pass with `mdsched.exe`, and switch off XMP and any overclock while it runs.

fixes.title: Uninstall third-party antivirus for now
fixes.detail: Remove the third-party security suite so its filter drivers are out of the picture, and keep Microsoft Defender turned on while you test.

fixes.title: Use Safe Mode if the PC keeps restarting
fixes.detail: From WinRE, go to Troubleshoot > Advanced options > Startup Settings > Restart and press 4 to enter Safe Mode. Uninstall the problem driver there, then restart normally.

prevention: Use a clean install when updating graphics and audio drivers
Set a restore point before every driver update
Keep beta and preview drivers off machines you depend on
Install Windows updates so older drivers receive compatibility fixes

title: PFN_LIST_CORRUPT
summary: Stop code 0x4E means the Page Frame Number (PFN) database, which the memory manager uses to track physical RAM, has become corrupted. The usual reasons are a driver writing to memory it does not own, or RAM that is starting to fail.
meaning: Windows keeps a record of every physical memory page in the PFN database. Stop 0x4E fires when one of those records turns out to be wrong, such as a page listed as free that is actually in use, or a list pointer leading nowhere. Only kernel components can modify this structure, so the cause almost always comes down to a driver overrunning its memory or failing RAM returning bad data. You will often see this error together with MEMORY_MANAGEMENT and PAGE_FAULT_IN_NONPAGED_AREA.
commonCauses: RAM that is defective or overclocked
A kernel-mode driver that corrupts memory
An unstable XMP or EXPO memory profile
Damaged system files
Other hardware faults, such as motherboard memory traces or controllers

fixes.title: Run Windows Memory Diagnostic
fixes.detail: Start `mdsched.exe` and pick the option to restart and check for problems. If the quick test comes back clean, run MemTest86 for several passes.

fixes.title: Turn off XMP or overclocking and test each stick alone
fixes.detail: Restore the BIOS defaults, then boot with a single memory module at a time to find a bad stick or slot.

fixes.title: Bring Windows and drivers up to date
fixes.detail: Install any waiting Windows updates and download fresh graphics, chipset and network drivers from the manufacturers' websites.

fixes.title: Repair system files with SFC and DISM
fixes.detail: In an elevated prompt, run `sfc /scannow`, then `DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth`, then `sfc /scannow` once more.

fixes.title: Check for malware
fixes.detail: A full Microsoft Defender scan will rule out malicious code tampering with kernel memory structures.

prevention: Test new memory thoroughly before relying on it every day
Do not mix memory modules that are not a matched set
Keep the BIOS and drivers updated
Run a stress test for several hours on any memory overclock

title: NTFS_FILE_SYSTEM
summary: Stop code 0x24 points to a failure inside Ntfs.sys, the driver that runs the NTFS file system. Either the volume is corrupted or the disk or storage driver broke down in the middle of an operation, and a dying drive is often the real reason.
meaning: Ntfs.sys is the kernel-mode driver behind the NTFS file system. Stop 0x24 means it ran into an inconsistency it had no way to resolve, such as damaged file system structures, a disk error during a write, or a bug in the storage driver. File system damage tends to spread, so treat this error as a warning about your data as well as a crash. Check the disk before you do anything else.
commonCauses: Corruption on the NTFS volume
A drive that is failing and developing bad sectors
Storage controller or driver bugs introduced by an update
A power cut during heavy disk writing
Loose or failing SATA or M.2 connections

fixes.title: Fix the volume with chkdsk
fixes.detail: Open an elevated prompt, run `chkdsk C: /f /r`, and allow the scan to run when Windows restarts. This is the main fix for this stop code.
fixes.riskNote: If the drive has already been slow or reporting errors, back up your important files before running it.

fixes.title: Check the health of the drive
fixes.detail: Run `wmic diskdrive get status`, look for disk errors in Event Viewer (System log, source 'disk'), and run the manufacturer's SMART utility. A drive showing reallocated or pending sectors should be replaced.

fixes.title: Repair system files with SFC and DISM
fixes.detail: Once chkdsk is done, fix system files by running `sfc /scannow` and `DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth`.

fixes.title: Update chipset and storage drivers
fixes.detail: Get the latest chipset and storage controller drivers from the manufacturers, particularly if the crashes began after a Windows feature update.

fixes.title: Back up your data right away if the error returns
fixes.detail: When NTFS_FILE_SYSTEM keeps coming back even after chkdsk, focus on copying your files off the drive and getting a replacement. Repeated file system crashes are a strong sign the disk is about to fail.

prevention: Protect against power loss during writes with a UPS, or keep a laptop's battery charged
Keep an eye on SMART data and retire aging drives
Run chkdsk whenever the PC shuts down improperly
Back up any files you cannot afford to lose

title: DRIVER_OVERRAN_STACK_BUFFER
summary: Stop code 0xF7 means a driver wrote beyond the end of a buffer on the stack and wiped out its check value. The kernel stopped immediately because a driver bug had corrupted kernel stack memory.
meaning: Every thread's kernel stack places guard values next to its buffers. When a driver writes past the end of a buffer, it overwrites that guard, and the kernel's security check catches the textbook buffer overrun and raises stop 0xF7. Windows shuts down at once because the stack can no longer be trusted. The driver that was running at the time is nearly always to blame, with corrupted system files and, less frequently, RAM making up the remaining causes.
commonCauses: A faulty kernel-mode driver, often one that was just updated
Damaged system files
Newly installed kernel-level software such as antivirus, VPN or system utilities
Defective RAM (a less frequent cause)
A driver that no longer works properly after a Windows feature update

fixes.title: Roll back or update drivers that changed recently
fixes.detail: If the crashes started after a driver or Windows update, use Device Manager to roll that driver back, or install the newest version from the manufacturer.

fixes.title: Repair system files with SFC and DISM
fixes.detail: In an elevated prompt, run `sfc /scannow`, then `DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth`, then `sfc /scannow` again. Restart afterward.

fixes.title: Remove recently installed software
fixes.detail: Uninstall security suites, VPN clients and system utilities that appeared just before the crashes. Restart between each removal so you can isolate the one responsible.

fixes.title: Test the RAM
fixes.detail: Run `mdsched.exe` to rule out memory corruption, keeping in mind that RAM is a less likely cause of this particular stop code.

fixes.title: Run Driver Verifier with special pool
fixes.detail: Start `verifier`, choose the standard settings plus special pool, and apply it to third-party drivers. This turns the overrun into an immediate crash that identifies the driver.
fixes.riskNote: Verifier intentionally crashes Windows when it catches the faulty driver, and a boot loop is possible. Turn it off by running `verifier /reset` from Safe Mode.

prevention: Update one driver at a time and create a restore point in between
Stay away from untrusted driver bundles and 'driver updater' programs
Keep Windows up to date
Run SFC after any unexpected shutdown

title: MACHINE_CHECK_EXCEPTION
summary: Stop code 0x9C means the processor reported a fatal machine-check error, a bus, cache or internal hardware fault that Windows cannot fix. Modern versions of Windows usually report the same kind of event as WHEA_UNCORRECTABLE_ERROR (0x124).
meaning: The processor raises a machine-check exception when it detects an internal problem it cannot recover from, such as a bus error, a cache parity failure or a memory controller fault. Windows receives that report and halts, since software cannot repair the hardware underneath. This is an older stop code. Current Windows routes these events through WHEA and reports them as stop 0x124, so seeing 0x9C generally suggests older hardware or older firmware paths.
commonCauses: A failing processor, motherboard or power supply
An unstable overclock or wrong or insufficient voltage
An overheating CPU or VRM
Defective RAM or memory controller problems
Outdated BIOS or CPU microcode

fixes.title: Remove overclocks and restore BIOS defaults
fixes.detail: Open BIOS/UEFI setup, load the optimized defaults, and undo any CPU, voltage or memory overclocking before you test anything else.

fixes.title: Update the BIOS/UEFI
fixes.detail: Install the newest firmware from your motherboard manufacturer. Updated microcode resolves genuine machine-check bugs on many platforms.
fixes.riskNote: If a firmware flash fails, it can brick the motherboard for good, so follow the manufacturer's procedure exactly.

fixes.title: Check temperatures, cooling and the power supply
fixes.detail: Watch CPU and VRM temperatures under load, clean out the cooling system, make sure every power connector is firmly seated, and try a known-good power supply if you have one.

fixes.title: Test the memory
fixes.detail: Run several passes of `mdsched.exe` or MemTest86. Test each stick on its own and try different slots.

fixes.title: Reseat parts and prepare to replace hardware
fixes.detail: Reseat the CPU cooler, memory and expansion cards. If machine checks keep happening at stock settings on the latest BIOS, the processor or motherboard has probably failed. Confirm with the manufacturer's diagnostics, then replace it.

prevention: Keep the BIOS and CPU microcode current
Clean out dust regularly and keep cooling in good shape
Choose a quality power supply with plenty of spare capacity
Do not run untested overclocks on machines you rely on

title: Windows Update error 0x80070002 (ERROR_FILE_NOT_FOUND)
summary: Error 0x80070002 ('The system cannot find the file specified') stops Windows Update when it cannot find or verify the files it needs to download or install an update. A damaged download cache or an incorrect system clock is usually behind it.
meaning: This code is a wrapper for the Win32 error ERROR_FILE_NOT_FOUND. While updating, Windows goes looking for downloaded payload files, servicing manifests or installation sources, and finds nothing usable. Common triggers include a corrupted or incomplete SoftwareDistribution download cache, a download that was cut off, a system clock that is set wrong, or proxy and security software removing files before the installer gets to them.
commonCauses: Damaged or partial files in the SoftwareDistribution download cache
An update download that was interrupted or timed out
Wrong date, time or region settings
A proxy, VPN or antivirus program interfering with the download
Corruption in the component store or system files

fixes.title: Run the Windows Update troubleshooter
fixes.detail: Go to Settings > System > Troubleshoot > Other troubleshooters (on Windows 10, Settings > Update & Security > Troubleshoot), run the Windows Update troubleshooter and accept the fixes it suggests.

fixes.title: Clear the update cache (SoftwareDistribution)
fixes.detail: Open an elevated Command Prompt and run `net stop wuauserv` and `net stop bits`. Rename `C:\Windows\SoftwareDistribution` to `SoftwareDistribution.old`, then run `net start bits` and `net start wuauserv` and try the update again.
fixes.riskNote: Only the download cache is cleared, so updates you already installed stay in place. You can delete the .old folder once updates work again.

fixes.title: Confirm the date, time and region
fixes.detail: In Settings > Time & language, turn on 'Set time automatically' and click to sync now. A clock that is off will break update validation and secure downloads.

fixes.title: Repair system files with SFC and DISM
fixes.detail: From an elevated prompt, run `sfc /scannow`, then `DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth`, then `sfc /scannow` again. This fixes the servicing files that updates rely on.

fixes.title: Install the update yourself from the Microsoft Update Catalog
fixes.detail: Look up the KB number of the failed update in Settings > Windows Update > Update history, search for it at catalog.update.microsoft.com, download the build that matches your edition of Windows, and run it directly.

prevention: Leave at least 10-20 GB of free space on the system drive
Never turn the PC off while updates are installing
Run the troubleshooter whenever an update fails
Keep automatic time synchronization turned on

title: Windows Update error 0x80073712 (ERROR_SXS_COMPONENT_STORE_CORRUPT)
summary: Error 0x80073712 ('The component store has been corrupted') means the WinSxS component store, where Windows stages and checks update files, is damaged, so servicing operations fail.
meaning: The code stands for ERROR_SXS_COMPONENT_STORE_CORRUPT. Windows builds updates out of trusted components kept in the WinSxS store, and that store is now damaged or inconsistent. Every installation is validated against it, which means a broken store blocks all servicing: cumulative updates, feature updates and .NET feature installs all fail. It usually shows up after interrupted updates, disk errors or a servicing process that crashed.
commonCauses: An earlier update that was interrupted or crashed during installation
Disk errors or bad sectors that damaged the store
Damaged system files
Too little free disk space while servicing was running
Malware or third-party software interfering with servicing

fixes.title: Fix the component store with DISM, followed by SFC
fixes.detail: From an elevated prompt, run `DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth` (an internet connection is required), then `sfc /scannow`, and try the update again. This is the main fix for a corrupted store.

fixes.title: Run the Windows Update troubleshooter
fixes.detail: Open Settings > System > Troubleshoot > Other troubleshooters > Windows Update (on Windows 10, Settings > Update & Security > Troubleshoot), apply what it recommends, and retry.

fixes.title: Clear the update cache (SoftwareDistribution)
fixes.detail: Run `net stop wuauserv` and `net stop bits`, rename `C:\Windows\SoftwareDistribution` to `SoftwareDistribution.old`, and then run `net start bits` and `net start wuauserv`.

fixes.title: Make room on the disk
fixes.detail: Keep at least 10-20 GB free on C: (use Settings > System > Storage > Cleanup recommendations). Servicing fails when the store has no room to grow.

fixes.title: Do an in-place repair upgrade as a last resort
fixes.detail: Get a Windows 11 or Windows 10 ISO, or use the Installation Assistant. Run setup and pick 'Keep personal files and apps' so Windows, including the component store, is rebuilt in place.
fixes.riskNote: The in-place upgrade is meant to keep your files, but back up personal data first anyway.

prevention: Let updates finish, and never cut power while servicing is underway
On PCs that crash often, run `DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /CheckHealth` from time to time
Keep more than 15-20% of the system drive free
Replace any drive that logs disk errors in Event Viewer

title: Windows Update error 0x800f0922
summary: Error 0x800f0922 shows up when a cumulative or feature update fails during installation. In most cases the PC cannot reach the Windows Update servers because of a proxy or VPN, or the hidden System Reserved partition is out of space.
meaning: This is a Component-Based Servicing (CBS) error, meaning the installer was unable to stage or finish one of the update packages. Microsoft points to two main causes: the PC cannot connect to the Windows Update servers, or the System Reserved partition is too small to hold the servicing files. A nearly full system drive, damaged components or a stuck earlier servicing session can produce the same code.
commonCauses: A System Reserved partition that is too small or completely full
A proxy or VPN that blocks access to the Windows Update servers
A damaged component store or a pending servicing operation
Too little free space on the system drive
A stuck servicing stack left behind by an earlier failed update

fixes.title: Turn off VPN and proxy, then try again
fixes.detail: Disconnect any VPN client and clear the proxy settings in Settings > Network & internet > Proxy, then run the update again. That step alone fixes many 0x800f0922 failures.

fixes.title: Make room on the disk
fixes.detail: Use Settings > System > Storage > Cleanup recommendations to free up 20 GB or more on C:, since feature updates need a lot of space.

fixes.title: Fix the component store with DISM and SFC
fixes.detail: From an elevated prompt, run `DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth`, then `sfc /scannow`, and retry the update.

fixes.title: Clear the update cache (SoftwareDistribution)
fixes.detail: Run `net stop wuauserv` and `net stop bits`, rename `C:\Windows\SoftwareDistribution` to `SoftwareDistribution.old`, and then run `net start bits` and `net start wuauserv`.

fixes.title: Install the update yourself from the Microsoft Update Catalog
fixes.detail: Find the KB number of the failed update in Settings > Windows Update > Update history, download that package from catalog.update.microsoft.com, and install it directly.

fixes.title: Fix or enlarge the System Reserved partition (advanced)
fixes.detail: When the System Reserved partition is full, you can enlarge it with a third-party partitioning tool or do a clean reinstall. Windows setup is not always able to grow it on its own.
fixes.riskNote: Resizing hidden partitions can leave the PC unable to boot. Back everything up first and follow a trusted guide step by step.

prevention: Leave 15-20% of the system drive free
Do not run feature upgrades over a VPN or proxy connection
Install servicing stack updates as soon as they are offered
Keep a backup image so you can recover from a failed upgrade

title: Windows Update error 0x8024402f (server error while connecting)
summary: Error 0x8024402f appears when the Windows Update client gets an error back from the server it is talking to. Usually the service is having a temporary problem, or a proxy, VPN or firewall on your side is getting in the way.
meaning: The code is WU_E_PT_HTTP_STATUS_SERVER_ERROR, which means the Windows Update Agent received an HTTP 500-range response from the update server or a gateway in front of it. Microsoft treats this as frequently temporary, for example when servers are busy or being maintained. If it keeps happening, look at the network path instead: a proxy, VPN, firewall or DNS problem, or a system clock so far off that secure connections fail.
commonCauses: A short-lived problem on Microsoft's servers (try again later)
A proxy, VPN or firewall interfering with update traffic
A wrong system date or time that breaks secure connections
DNS trouble on the local network
A damaged Windows Update cache on the PC

fixes.title: Wait a while, then retry
fixes.detail: Since the server side is often the cause, give it 30-60 minutes and check for updates again before you change any settings.

fixes.title: Confirm your connection and turn off VPN and proxy
fixes.detail: Make sure websites load normally, disconnect any VPN, and switch off proxy settings in Settings > Network & internet > Proxy. Then try again.

fixes.title: Check the date and time
fixes.detail: In Settings > Time & language, turn on 'Set time automatically' and click 'Sync now'. A clock that is out of sync breaks the secure connection to the update servers.

fixes.title: Flush DNS and reboot the router
fixes.detail: Run `ipconfig /flushdns` in an elevated prompt, then restart your router or network gear. This clears stale DNS entries that can send the update client to a bad server.

fixes.title: Use the troubleshooter, then clear the update cache
fixes.detail: Run the Windows Update troubleshooter from Settings > System > Troubleshoot > Other troubleshooters. Then reset the cache with `net stop wuauserv`, `net stop bits`, rename `C:\Windows\SoftwareDistribution` to `SoftwareDistribution.old`, `net start bits`, `net start wuauserv`.

fixes.title: Repair system files if nothing else works
fixes.detail: Run `sfc /scannow` and then `DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth` to make sure the update client itself is not damaged.

prevention: When the problem is a temporary network or server issue, simply retry instead of changing lots of settings
Leave date and time on automatic
On corporate proxies, allow the Windows Update endpoints
Run SFC and DISM checks now and then to keep the update client healthy

title: Windows Update error 0x80240034 (download failure)
summary: Error 0x80240034 means the update download did not succeed: the package could not be retrieved, checked or finished. An unreliable connection, a damaged download cache or a problem on Microsoft's end is usually responsible.
meaning: The code is WU_E_DOWNLOAD_FAILED and it is raised during the download phase. Either Windows could not finish transferring the update package, or the package it received did not pass verification. Weak Wi-Fi, metered connection settings, interference from a proxy or VPN, a stuck SoftwareDistribution cache and overloaded Microsoft servers can all produce it.
commonCauses: A weak or dropping internet connection
Damaged files in the SoftwareDistribution download cache
A proxy, VPN or antivirus program interfering with the download
A metered connection setting that blocks big downloads
Problems on the Windows Update servers

fixes.title: Run the Windows Update troubleshooter
fixes.detail: Open Settings > System > Troubleshoot > Other troubleshooters > Windows Update (on Windows 10, Settings > Update & Security > Troubleshoot), accept its fixes, and try again.

fixes.title: Clear the update cache (SoftwareDistribution)
fixes.detail: From an elevated prompt run `net stop wuauserv`, `net stop bits`, rename `C:\Windows\SoftwareDistribution` to `SoftwareDistribution.old`, `net start bits`, `net start wuauserv`, and then check for updates again.

fixes.title: Check the connection and the metered setting
fixes.detail: Make sure the network is stable (a wired Ethernet connection is a good test) and turn off 'Metered connection' in Settings > Network & internet > Wi-Fi so large downloads can go through.

fixes.title: Repair system files with SFC and DISM
fixes.detail: Run `sfc /scannow` and then `DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth`, and try the update once more.

fixes.title: Install the update yourself from the Microsoft Update Catalog
fixes.detail: Look up the failed KB in your update history, download the matching package from catalog.update.microsoft.com and run it. This skips the Windows Update download process completely.

prevention: Download large updates over a reliable connection
On unlimited networks, leave the metered connection option off
Keep 10-20 GB of free space on the system drive
Retry a download failure that looks temporary before trying bigger fixes

title: Windows Update error 0x8007000d (ERROR_INVALID_DATA)
summary: Error 0x8007000d ('The data is invalid') means an update package or data in the component store did not pass validation. In nearly every case, the download or the servicing files are corrupted.
meaning: This code wraps the Win32 error ERROR_INVALID_DATA. During an update, it tells you Windows inspected update data and found it malformed. That can be a corrupted download, damaged entries in the component store, or bad disk sectors in the servicing path. It often follows a download that was cut short, a power loss during servicing, or a drive that is starting to develop bad sectors.
commonCauses: An update download that arrived corrupted
Corruption in the WinSxS component store
Disk errors or bad sectors affecting the servicing files
An installation interrupted by a crash or power loss
A drive that is starting to fail

fixes.title: Run the Windows Update troubleshooter
fixes.detail: Open Settings > System > Troubleshoot > Other troubleshooters > Windows Update, apply its suggestions, and retry.

fixes.title: Fix the component store with DISM, followed by SFC
fixes.detail: From an elevated prompt, run `DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth` and then `sfc /scannow`. DISM restores the damaged data that updates are checked against.

fixes.title: Clear the update cache (SoftwareDistribution)
fixes.detail: Run `net stop wuauserv`, `net stop bits`, rename `C:\Windows\SoftwareDistribution` to `SoftwareDistribution.old`, `net start bits`, `net start wuauserv`, and then try the update again.

fixes.title: Scan the drive for errors
fixes.detail: Run `chkdsk C: /f /r` and let it scan during the next restart. Bad sectors in the servicing area will trigger this error on every attempt.
fixes.riskNote: If the drive has shown other signs of failing, back up your important files first.

fixes.title: Install the update yourself from the Microsoft Update Catalog
fixes.detail: Get the failed KB from catalog.update.microsoft.com and install it directly, which replaces the corrupted package.

prevention: Avoid losing power during updates, and use a UPS when you can
Keep track of drive health and replace failing disks early
Run a DISM CheckHealth after any unexpected shutdown
Keep 10-20 GB of free space on the system drive

title: Windows Update error 0x8024a105 (installation stuck or failed)
summary: Error 0x8024a105 shows up when an update sits at 'Pending install' or fails while installing. The download is usually fine: the real cause tends to be a stuck servicing state, low disk space or a conflict with other running software.
meaning: This code is part of the Windows Update Agent's install-stage error group. The download finished, but the installer could not apply the package, or the update stays stuck at 'Pending install' or 'Pending restart'. The common background is a servicing state that never cleared, not enough free space, or interference from third-party software, antivirus in particular.
commonCauses: A servicing state left stuck or pending by an earlier update
Not enough free disk space to stage the installation
Interference from third-party antivirus or system utilities
A damaged Windows Update cache
A restart that is still pending and blocks the next step

fixes.title: Restart, then try the update again
fixes.detail: Do a proper restart (not a shutdown with Fast Startup) and check for updates again. A pending install often sorts itself out after a reboot.

fixes.title: Run the Windows Update troubleshooter
fixes.detail: Open Settings > System > Troubleshoot > Other troubleshooters > Windows Update and let it reset stuck components and apply its fixes.

fixes.title: Clear the update cache (SoftwareDistribution)
fixes.detail: From an elevated prompt run `net stop wuauserv`, `net stop bits`, rename `C:\Windows\SoftwareDistribution` to `SoftwareDistribution.old`, `net start bits`, `net start wuauserv`.

fixes.title: Make room on the disk
fixes.detail: Free up 10-20 GB on C: (Settings > System > Storage > Cleanup recommendations) so the installer has room to stage its files.

fixes.title: Turn off third-party antivirus for now and install manually
fixes.detail: Disable or remove the third-party security suite while the update installs, or download the failed KB from catalog.update.microsoft.com and install it yourself.
fixes.riskNote: Turn your antivirus back on as soon as the update is finished.

prevention: When Windows says a restart is pending, restart instead of putting it off again and again
Keep 10-20 GB of free space on the system drive
Do not use third-party tools that block updates
Pause updates through Settings when you need to, instead of disabling services

title: Windows Update error 0x80070020 (ERROR_SHARING_VIOLATION)
summary: Error 0x80070020 ('The process cannot access the file because it is being used by another process') means a file the installer needs is locked. Antivirus, backup or sync software is usually holding it.
meaning: This code wraps the Win32 error ERROR_SHARING_VIOLATION. To replace system files, Windows Update needs exclusive access to them, and some other process has them open. The usual lock holders are real-time antivirus scanners, backup agents, cloud sync tools, or a second update running at the same time. Once whatever is holding the file gets out of the way, the error goes away.
commonCauses: Third-party antivirus scanning or locking the update files
Backup or cloud sync software keeping system files open
A second installer or update running at the same time
A process left hanging by an earlier failed update
Utilities that monitor system files

fixes.title: Restart the PC and try the update again
fixes.detail: A full restart frees locked files and ends stuck installer processes. For a sharing violation, it is the easiest step and often the one that works.

fixes.title: Turn off third-party antivirus for now
fixes.detail: Pause or uninstall the third-party security suite while you update (Microsoft Defender will take over on its own), try again, and turn protection back on afterward.
fixes.riskNote: Do not leave the PC unprotected. Turn antivirus back on right after the test.

fixes.title: Do a clean boot
fixes.detail: Run `msconfig` and choose 'Selective startup'. On the Services tab, tick 'Hide all Microsoft services' and click Disable all. Restart, run the update, and then go back to normal startup.

fixes.title: Run the Windows Update troubleshooter
fixes.detail: Open Settings > System > Troubleshoot > Other troubleshooters > Windows Update. It finds and repairs stuck update components.

fixes.title: Clear the update cache (SoftwareDistribution)
fixes.detail: Run `net stop wuauserv`, `net stop bits`, rename `C:\Windows\SoftwareDistribution` to `SoftwareDistribution.old`, `net start bits`, `net start wuauserv`. This removes files still locked by an installer that has crashed.

prevention: Pause backup and sync software while you install updates
Install only one real-time security product
Wait for one update to finish before you start another installation
Restart after a failed update before you try again

title: Windows upgrade error 0xC1900101 (setup rolled back because of a driver)
summary: You start a feature update, such as moving from Windows 10 to Windows 11 or installing a major version upgrade, and after a long wait Windows reverts to where it was and shows 0xC1900101. Something about a driver or a piece of hardware broke setup during or shortly after installation, so Windows reversed the upgrade.
meaning: Think of 0xC1900101 as an umbrella code that says setup failed and is rolling back. Setup lays down the new version of Windows, then runs into a driver (typically graphics, storage or network) or a hardware fault that misbehaves in the new environment. Rather than leave you with a broken system, it restores the previous version automatically. Your files survive, but the upgrade cannot finish. The second code shown alongside it (for example 0xC1900101 - 0x20017) tells you which phase of setup failed.
commonCauses: Graphics, storage or network drivers that are old or not compatible with the new version
A third-party antivirus product that conflicts with setup
Not enough free space on the system drive to stage the upgrade
An unreliable or failing peripheral plugged in while setup runs
Motherboard BIOS or UEFI firmware that predates the new Windows release

fixes.title: Bring the main drivers up to date first
fixes.detail: While still on your current version of Windows, download the latest graphics, chipset/storage and network drivers from each hardware maker's website and install them. Then launch setup again.

fixes.title: Remove any third-party antivirus
fixes.detail: Uninstall the third-party security suite before you upgrade. Microsoft Defender takes over protection while setup runs. Once the upgrade succeeds, install a version of the suite that supports Windows 11.

fixes.title: Unplug peripherals you don't need
fixes.detail: Disconnect USB drives, docking stations, printers and any secondary graphics card you can do without. A driver for one of these devices is a frequent reason setup decides to roll back.

fixes.title: Make room on the system drive
fixes.detail: Aim for at least 20 GB of free space on the system drive. Settings > System > Storage > Cleanup recommendations is a quick way to get there. If space runs out partway through, setup aborts the upgrade.

fixes.title: Install the latest BIOS/UEFI firmware
fixes.detail: Check your PC or motherboard maker's support page and apply the newest firmware before attempting a major upgrade. Outdated firmware is a known cause of 0xC1900101 rollbacks.
fixes.riskNote: Stick to the manufacturer's update instructions step by step. If a firmware flash is interrupted or fails, the board may no longer boot.

fixes.title: Try again with the Installation Assistant or an ISO, then read the setup log
