fixes.title: Start once without signature enforcement (if Windows will not boot)
fixes.detail: In the recovery environment, go to Troubleshoot > Advanced options > Startup Settings > Restart, then press 7 or F7 to start one time with driver signature enforcement turned off. Uninstall the problem driver right away, then restart normally.
fixes.riskNote: Turning off signature checks weakens security. Use it only long enough to remove the bad driver, and never leave the PC running that way.

fixes.title: Repair Windows files with SFC and DISM
fixes.detail: If the blocked file belongs to Windows itself, open an elevated prompt and run `sfc /scannow` and `DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth` to replace it with the genuine signed version.

fixes.title: Review Secure Boot after firmware changes
fixes.detail: If the error began after you changed BIOS or UEFI settings, load the firmware defaults while keeping the same boot mode, so the Secure Boot key databases load properly. Then test again.
fixes.riskNote: Record every original firmware setting first. Incorrect changes can affect booting and virtualization features.

prevention: Download drivers only from the manufacturer's site, where signatures are current
Avoid 'driver pack' tools and test-signed builds
Keep Windows updated, because certificate revocation lists arrive through Windows Update
Make a restore point before installing software that includes kernel drivers, such as VPNs, anti-cheat tools, and peripheral suites

title: WDF_VIOLATION (0x0000010D)
summary: WDF_VIOLATION (0x0000010D) is a blue screen that happens when a driver breaks the rules of the Windows Driver Framework. A buggy driver for a peripheral is usually to blame, such as keyboard or RGB software, Bluetooth, or a USB device.
meaning: WDF means Windows Driver Frameworks, which covers KMDF and UMDF. If a driver built on the framework mishandles its objects, handles, or queues, the kernel stops with bug check 0x0000010D, and the parameters describe exactly which rule was broken. In practice the offender is almost always a third-party driver that came with a keyboard, mouse, headset, printer, or similar device, and it often surfaces after a Windows update changes how the framework behaves.
commonCauses: A buggy third-party driver included with peripheral software (RGB, macro, or audio utilities)
An older framework-based driver that a Windows update broke
Several vendor utilities stacking conflicting filter drivers onto the same device
A driver installation that was corrupted by a failed update
Failing hardware that pushes its driver into error-handling paths

fixes.title: Uninstall the peripheral software or driver you added most recently
fixes.detail: Remove whatever keyboard, mouse, audio, or printer suite or driver you installed just before the crashes began, then restart. That step clears up most WDF_VIOLATION cases on its own.

fixes.title: Use Safe Mode if the blue screen keeps repeating
fixes.detail: If Windows crashes every time it starts, open WinRE (through Settings > System > Recovery > Advanced startup, or by interrupting startup three times). Choose Troubleshoot > Advanced options > Startup Settings > Restart, press 4 for Safe Mode, and remove the problem driver from there.

fixes.title: Install the vendor's latest driver for the device
fixes.detail: Download the current driver for the affected device from its manufacturer and install it. Many vendors released fixes for WDF violations after framework changes in Windows 10 and 11.

fixes.title: Check system files with SFC and DISM
fixes.detail: In an elevated prompt, run `sfc /scannow`, then `DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth`, to make sure the Windows framework files are not damaged.

fixes.title: Find the bad driver with Driver Verifier (advanced)
fixes.detail: Launch `verifier`, choose the standard settings, and select the non-Microsoft drivers. The guilty driver will crash right away and appear by name on the blue screen. Turn Verifier off when you are done with `verifier /reset`.
fixes.riskNote: Driver Verifier deliberately causes blue screens for suspect drivers. Make sure you know how to reach Safe Mode and run `verifier /reset` before turning it on.

fixes.title: Read the minidumps to spot repeat offenders (advanced)
fixes.detail: If the crashes continue, open the files in C:\Windows\Minidump with WinDbg and run `!analyze -v` to see which driver is named. Then update or remove the software that installed it.

prevention: Only install a peripheral maker's software if you actually use its features
Do not run several RGB or macro utilities from different brands at once
Make a restore point before updating drivers
Keep Windows updated so you receive framework fixes

title: Kernel-Power Event ID 41 (Critical)
codes: The system has rebooted without cleanly shutting down first
summary: When Windows restarts without shutting down properly, it writes a critical Kernel-Power Event ID 41 on the next boot. The entry tells you the PC either lost power or crashed hard, but it is a record of the symptom rather than the name of one specific fault.
meaning: On the next startup after an improper shutdown, Kernel-Power logs Event 41 under Windows Logs > System in Event Viewer. That covers a sudden loss of power, a frozen system that someone reset by holding the power button, and crashes so severe that Windows had no chance to save its state. The event data records what the machine was doing when it went down. Seeing a single 41 after a power outage is nothing to worry about. When the event keeps coming back, the usual suspects are an unstable overclock, faulty RAM, a weak power supply, or heat.
commonCauses: An overclock or XMP memory profile that is not fully stable
A power supply (PSU) that is failing or too small for the hardware
CPU, GPU, or VRM temperatures high enough to trigger a protective hard shutdown
A driver or hardware crash so abrupt that Windows never gets to shut down cleanly
Problems with incoming power, such as outages, bad power strips, or a worn-out laptop battery

fixes.title: Look for a pattern in Event Viewer
fixes.detail: In Event Viewer, go to Windows Logs > System and line up each Event 41 with whatever was logged right before it, especially Event 1001 (BugCheck) and WHEA entries. If a BugCheck comes first, you are most likely dealing with a driver problem or BSOD. If the 41 shows up with nothing ahead of it, focus on power delivery or hardware.

fixes.title: Turn off overclocking and XMP
fixes.detail: Open BIOS/UEFI setup and load the default settings, or at minimum switch your memory from XMP/EXPO back to standard JEDEC speeds. Run the PC that way for a few days to confirm it is stable before you start tuning again.
fixes.riskNote: Firmware changes can stop the PC from booting. Take photos or notes of your current BIOS settings before you touch anything.

fixes.title: Check memory using Windows Memory Diagnostic
fixes.detail: Launch `mdsched.exe`, pick the restart option, and let the extended test run all the way through. If it reports any errors, test each RAM stick on its own or leave MemTest86 running overnight.

fixes.title: Watch temperatures while the PC is working hard
fixes.detail: Keep a hardware monitoring tool open while gaming or running a stress test, and track CPU and GPU temperatures. If the readings climb sharply just before a shutdown, clean out the coolers, replace the thermal paste, or improve airflow through the case.

fixes.title: Bring BIOS, chipset, and GPU drivers up to date
fixes.detail: Install the latest stable BIOS from your motherboard maker along with current chipset drivers, since firmware updates fix a lot of hard-hang bugs. While flashing, keep the PC on a dependable outlet or a UPS.
fixes.riskNote: If a BIOS flash fails, the motherboard can be left unusable. Stick exactly to the vendor's instructions and make sure power is not cut during the update.

fixes.title: Consider the PSU if reboots keep happening
fixes.detail: Sudden reboots under load, even with normal temperatures and RAM that passes testing, usually point to a power supply that is failing or lacks the wattage you need. Swap in a known-good PSU with enough capacity, or take the PC to a repair shop.

prevention: Pick a good-quality PSU rated comfortably above what your system draws at peak
Clean out dust and check that every fan works about twice a year
Skip one-click auto-overclocking tools, and stress-test any manual tuning you do
If your local power is unreliable, run the PC from a UPS

title: WHEA-Logger Event ID 18: Corrected hardware error
codes: A corrected hardware error has occurred
summary: WHEA-Logger Event ID 18 means the hardware hit an error and corrected it on its own, usually in a CPU core or cache. Nothing crashed, but the event typically signals instability from voltage settings or overclocking.
meaning: The Windows Hardware Error Architecture (WHEA) writes Event 18 with the text 'A corrected hardware error has occurred' and usually lists Component: Processor Core. The processor's built-in error correction caught the fault and repaired it, so the system kept running. Repeated entries are an early sign of instability, though. Classic causes are adaptive undervolts or overclocks on Intel chips, borderline RAM, and VRM trouble. If you ignore them, they often turn into crashes and blue screens later.
commonCauses: An undervolt or overclock that is not stable, with Intel adaptive/LLC undervolting a frequent offender
RAM that is borderline, or an XMP/EXPO profile pushed too hard
A CPU, motherboard VRM, or power delivery circuit that is wearing out
Excess heat around the CPU or the VRM area
An outdated BIOS or microcode version with documented stability bugs

fixes.title: Load BIOS defaults and undo any undervolting
fixes.detail: Restore BIOS defaults and switch off every undervolt or overclock profile, including undervolts set in XTU or other vendor utilities. Keep an eye on Event Viewer for a few days. If Event 18 no longer appears, the voltage tuning was the cause.
fixes.riskNote: Before resetting, write down or photograph your current BIOS settings so you can restore them on purpose later.

fixes.title: Install the latest BIOS/firmware
fixes.detail: Get the newest BIOS from your motherboard manufacturer. Microcode in these updates often fixes processor error reporting and stability problems. Keep the PC on reliable power during the flash.
fixes.riskNote: If the flash fails, the board can end up bricked. Do exactly what the vendor's instructions say.

fixes.title: Run a memory test
fixes.detail: Use `mdsched.exe` (Windows Memory Diagnostic) or leave MemTest86 running overnight. If errors appear, test one stick at a time and replace whichever one is bad.

fixes.title: Check cooling and airflow
fixes.detail: Clean the coolers, make sure every fan is spinning, and watch CPU and package temperatures under load. An overheating CPU and hot VRMs can both trigger corrected hardware errors.

fixes.title: Move on to hardware diagnosis if errors continue at stock settings
fixes.detail: If Event 18 keeps appearing with default settings and current firmware, test the CPU and motherboard outside the case with a minimal setup, then start a warranty claim for whichever part is at fault.

prevention: Stick to voltage settings you have proven stable, and stress-test every tuning change
Install BIOS updates that list stability fixes
Keep coolers clean and the case well ventilated
Look into WHEA events as soon as they show up rather than dismissing them
Check Event Viewer every so often, since corrected errors never show a message on screen

title: A disk read error occurred (0xc00000e9)
codes: An unexpected I/O error has occurred
summary: The message 'A disk read error occurred. Press Ctrl+Alt+Del to restart', often shown with 0xc00000e9, means startup could not read data from the disk. The cause could be the drive itself, a cable, a connection, or the boot order.
meaning: The boot loader tried to read data it needs from your storage device and failed. The 'unexpected I/O error' version of the message comes with code 0xC00000E9. The cause can be minor, like a USB stick listed ahead of the Windows disk in the boot order or a SATA cable that worked loose, or it can be serious, like a drive developing unreadable sectors. Deal with it quickly, because it can be an early warning that the drive is about to fail completely.
commonCauses: An HDD or SSD with bad or unreadable sectors
A SATA data or power cable that is loose or damaged
A boot order that tries a non-bootable USB device or a dead disk first
File system or disk errors left behind by a sudden power cut
Failing electronics or a failing controller on the drive

fixes.title: Remove USB storage and review the boot order
fixes.detail: Unplug every USB storage device and card reader, then restart. If Windows starts, open firmware setup and put the Windows disk first in the boot order.

fixes.title: Reseat or swap the drive cables (desktops)
fixes.detail: With the power off, unplug and firmly reconnect the SATA data and power cables at the drive and the motherboard, or replace them with cables you know work. On a laptop with an accessible drive bay, reseat the drive or M.2 module.

fixes.title: Use Startup Repair in the recovery environment
fixes.detail: Get into WinRE, either by interrupting startup three times or by booting a Windows installation USB and choosing Repair your computer. Then go to Troubleshoot > Advanced options > Startup Repair.

fixes.title: Copy your important files right away
fixes.detail: As soon as you can get into Windows, or from the Command Prompt in WinRE, copy any files you cannot replace to another drive or a cloud service. Read errors during startup often mean the drive is about to fail.

fixes.title: Test the disk with chkdsk and SMART
fixes.detail: From an elevated Command Prompt or from WinRE, run `chkdsk C: /f /r`. Then check the drive's SMART attributes, especially reallocated and pending sector counts, using the manufacturer's tool or CrystalDiskInfo.
fixes.riskNote: A drive that already has read errors may fail completely under chkdsk's full surface scan. Make your backup first.

fixes.title: Clone the failing drive and replace it
fixes.detail: If SMART reports reallocated or pending sectors, clone the disk to a new drive with the manufacturer's software or a disk cloning tool, then swap the new drive in. Clone as soon as you can, before the old drive degrades further.
fixes.riskNote: The drive could die partway through cloning, so save your most important files before you start a full clone.

prevention: Set up automatic backups so a dead drive is a hassle, not a disaster
Check SMART health on every drive from time to time
Use a UPS and good cables, and never move a drive while it is powered
Replace a drive as soon as it shows early warning signs instead of waiting for it to fail

title: No audio output device is enabled
codes: No audio output device is enabled
no audio output device is installed
summary: When the speaker icon has a red X and Windows says 'No audio output device is enabled' (or 'is installed'), the sound hardware is either disabled, missing its driver, or not detected at all.
meaning: Windows has no audio endpoints to list because the audio controller or its driver is not running. The device might have been disabled, an update may have broken the driver, the audio services may have stopped, or, in rare cases, the audio hardware has failed. Your speakers and headphones will not appear as outputs until the driver and its endpoints are working again.
commonCauses: A Windows update that broke or removed the audio driver
The device being disabled in Device Manager or in Sound settings
The Windows Audio or Windows Audio Endpoint Builder service not running
The onboard audio controller switched off in BIOS/UEFI
A hardware failure in the audio chip (uncommon)

fixes.title: Look for disabled outputs in Sound settings
fixes.detail: Go to Settings > System > Sound and, if any devices appear, choose the correct output. Next, open the classic Control Panel > Sound and go to the Playback tab. Right-click a blank area, select 'Show Disabled Devices', enable your speakers or headphones, and make them the default.

fixes.title: Restart the audio services
fixes.detail: Open `services.msc` and restart 'Windows Audio' and 'Windows Audio Endpoint Builder'. Make sure both have their startup type set to Automatic, then restart the PC.

fixes.title: Rescan or reinstall the audio device in Device Manager
fixes.detail: Expand 'Sound, video and game controllers' and 'Audio inputs and outputs', and enable anything that is disabled. You can also choose Action > Scan for hardware changes, or right-click the device, pick Uninstall device, and restart so Windows reinstalls the driver.

fixes.title: Install the manufacturer's audio driver
fixes.detail: Download the audio driver (Realtek, Conexant, or Intel SST, for example) from your laptop or motherboard manufacturer's website and install it. After a big Windows update, the generic Microsoft driver sometimes fails to create the output endpoints.

fixes.title: Try the audio troubleshooter
fixes.detail: Go to Settings > System > Troubleshoot > Other troubleshooters, find Playing Audio, select Run, and apply any fixes it suggests.

fixes.title: Check BIOS when the audio controller has disappeared
fixes.detail: If Device Manager lists no audio controller at all, open firmware setup and make sure onboard audio (often labeled HD Audio) is enabled.
fixes.riskNote: Write down the original BIOS settings before you change anything.

prevention: Keep a copy of the manufacturer's audio driver, and create a restore point before installing a feature update
When tidying up sound settings, avoid disabling playback devices
Leave the Windows Audio services on their default startup type
If sound breaks right after a driver update, roll the audio driver back

title: Disk usage stuck at 100% in Task Manager
summary: The Disk column in Task Manager stays at or near 100% and everything on the PC slows to a crawl. This is the classic sign of a saturated drive, and sometimes it means the disk is failing.
meaning: If active time stays at 100%, the drive's request queue is full: work comes in faster than the disk can complete it. On a mechanical hard drive, ordinary background activity such as Search indexing, SysMain (formerly Superfetch), Windows Update, and antivirus scans can be enough to max it out. On an SSD, the same reading more often points to a software problem or a failing drive that keeps retrying slow sectors.
commonCauses: A hard drive buried under background work like SysMain/Superfetch, Search indexing, Windows Update, or Defender scans
A failing drive slowed down by repeated retries on bad sectors (check SMART)
Malware or a cryptominer constantly reading from and writing to the disk
Cloud sync software repeatedly syncing large folders
Not enough RAM, which forces Windows to page to disk all the time

fixes.title: Find out which process is using the disk
fixes.detail: Press Ctrl+Shift+Esc to open Task Manager, go to Processes, and sort by the Disk column. Check what is at the top. If it is a normal background job such as an update, the indexer, or a sync client, let it finish or pause it before you start changing system settings.

fixes.title: Check the health of the drive
fixes.detail: Open an elevated Command Prompt and run `chkdsk C: /f` to fix file system errors. Then look at the SMART data (reallocated and pending sectors) with the drive maker's utility or CrystalDiskInfo. A failing drive produces exactly this symptom.

fixes.title: Check for malware
fixes.detail: Run a full scan in Windows Security (Virus & threat protection > Scan options > Full scan). It is worth doing whenever 100% disk usage continues with no clear explanation or unfamiliar processes show up.

fixes.title: Stop SysMain temporarily as a test
fixes.detail: In `services.msc`, stop the SysMain service (formerly Superfetch) and set its startup type to Disabled for a while. If an HDD-based system feels smoother afterward, you can leave it off or plan to move to an SSD.

fixes.title: Reduce startup apps
fixes.detail: Open Task Manager > Startup apps and disable anything you do not need at startup, such as sync clients, updaters, and helper tools. That reduces the disk load during boot.

fixes.title: Move Windows to an SSD (the best long-term fix)
fixes.detail: If Windows is on a hard drive, cloning it to an SSD makes the system far more responsive and practically ends this problem. Use the SSD maker's cloning software, and confirm the new drive boots before you erase the old one.
fixes.riskNote: You will be opening the PC and moving data between drives. Make sure the clone works before you format anything.

prevention: Install Windows on an SSD
Keep about 15-20% of the system drive free
Cut down on startup programs and background sync tools
Check SMART health regularly so you spot a dying drive early

title: High CPU usage from Windows Explorer (explorer.exe)
summary: Task Manager shows explorer.exe using a lot of CPU. The Windows shell (desktop, taskbar, and File Explorer) is stuck in a loop, often because of a corrupt thumbnail cache or a third-party shell extension.
meaning: explorer.exe draws the desktop, the taskbar, and every File Explorer window. When it keeps using a lot of CPU, it is usually redrawing or rereading something over and over. Typical causes are a corrupt icon or thumbnail cache, a buggy third-party shell extension (cloud sync overlay icons or archive tools in the right-click menu), constant attempts to refresh network drives that are unavailable, or a known Windows 11 Explorer bug that a cumulative update has since fixed.
commonCauses: Icon and thumbnail caches that have become corrupt
Buggy third-party shell extensions, such as cloud overlay icons or right-click menu tools
Explorer or taskbar bugs in Windows 11 that later cumulative updates fixed
Network drives that are slow or unreachable, so Explorer keeps refreshing them
Widgets or taskbar components that are malfunctioning

fixes.title: Restart Windows Explorer
fixes.detail: In Task Manager, find 'Windows Explorer' (explorer.exe) and choose Restart. The desktop and taskbar disappear for a moment and come back. This quick reset often breaks the loop.

fixes.title: Install pending Windows updates
fixes.detail: Open Settings > Windows Update and install every cumulative update that is waiting. Microsoft fixed several Windows 11 Explorer CPU bugs through these updates.

fixes.title: Delete the icon and thumbnail caches
fixes.detail: Close all File Explorer windows. In Task Manager, start a Command Prompt (File > Run new task > `cmd`), then end explorer.exe. Delete the `thumbcache_*.db` and `iconcache*.db` files in %localappdata%\Microsoft\Windows\Explorer, plus %localappdata%\IconCache.db, and then start explorer.exe again. Windows rebuilds the caches automatically.

fixes.title: Find the problem shell extension
fixes.detail: Do a clean boot (`msconfig` > hide all Microsoft services > disable the rest), or use a shell extension manager to turn off non-Microsoft context menu and overlay extensions. Turn them back on a few at a time until the CPU spike returns, which tells you which one is responsible.

fixes.title: Remove mapped drives that no longer work
fixes.detail: Go to File Explorer > This PC and disconnect any drive mapped to a server that is offline or gone (right-click > Disconnect). Explorer will stop polling paths it cannot reach.

prevention: Install Windows 11 cumulative updates as they come out
Only keep shell extension tools (overlay icons, context menu add-ons) you actually use
Remove mapped network drives that no longer work
If Explorer gets stuck in a loop, restart it instead of leaving it running for hours

title: 0xC004C060: Product key blocked or activation limit exceeded
summary: Error 0xC004C060 means Microsoft's activation servers refused the product key. The key has either been blocked or has run out of allowed activations, which happens a lot with volume license (MAK) keys.
meaning: The failure happened on Microsoft's side: the key was either blocked by Microsoft or has been activated more times than it allows. Retail keys rarely hit this. Volume license MAK keys come with a fixed number of activations, and keys that leak or get resold against the license terms end up blocked. If you bought a key and see this error, it is often a gray-market volume key and not a real retail key.
commonCauses: A Multiple Activation Key (MAK) with no activations left
A key Microsoft blocked after it leaked or was abused
A volume license key sold to individual buyers, which the license terms do not allow
Hardware changes that used up the remaining activations on the key
Trying to activate on more PCs than the license covers

fixes.title: Check your current activation status
fixes.detail: Open Settings > System > Activation and read the exact status message. In an elevated Command Prompt, `slmgr /xpr` tells you whether the current license is permanent or expires. That is helpful to know before you change anything.

fixes.title: Use the Activation troubleshooter
fixes.detail: In Settings > System > Activation, select Troubleshoot. If the PC was activated before and its digital license is linked to a Microsoft account, the troubleshooter can reactivate it after a hardware change.

fixes.title: Try again later or ask whoever owns the license
fixes.detail: On a work or school device, contact IT, since your licensing administrator can get the MAK activation limit raised. Temporary problems on Microsoft's servers can also clear if you try again a day later.

fixes.title: Activate by phone
fixes.detail: Run `slui 4`, choose your country, and follow the prompts for phone activation. The call goes to an automated licensing line and can work even when online activation is refused.

fixes.title: Replace a purchased key that has been blocked
fixes.detail: If a key you bought turns out to be blocked, ask the seller for a refund and buy a new one from an authorized retailer. Microsoft support can tell you whether the key is genuine and whether it has been blocked.

prevention: Buy product keys only from Microsoft or from authorized retailers
Keep your proof of purchase and a record of the key somewhere safe
For organizations: watch MAK activation counts in the Volume Licensing Service Center
Link your digital license to a Microsoft account to make reactivation easy

title: 0xC004F074: Key Management Service (KMS) could not be contacted
codes: Key Management Service could not be contacted
The Key Management Server (KMS) is unavailable
summary: Error 0xC004F074 means Windows could not contact a Key Management Service (KMS) host to activate. It is a licensing server, network, or DNS problem, and it shows up mostly on volume-licensed corporate PCs.
meaning: Volume-licensed copies of Windows activate against an internal KMS host, which they find through DNS records. If the PC cannot reach that host, activation fails with 0xC004F074. Common reasons are being off the corporate network, a missing DNS SRV record, a KMS host that is down, or a clock that is badly wrong. On personal computers, the error often appears after someone has used or removed a pirate KMS 'activator', because those tools fake a local KMS host.
commonCauses: The PC cannot reach the corporate KMS host (not on the VPN or on the wrong network)
The DNS SRV record (_vlmcs._tcp) for the KMS host is missing or wrong
The KMS host is offline, or its own license has expired
The system clock is far enough off that the activation exchange fails
Leftovers from an unauthorized KMS 'activator' tool on a personal PC

fixes.title: Check activation status and your network connection
fixes.detail: Read the exact message in Settings > System > Activation. Make sure you are connected to the corporate network or VPN, then run `ipconfig /all` and check that the DNS servers listed are your company's.

fixes.title: Check the system clock
fixes.detail: Make sure the date, time, and time zone are correct in Settings > Time & language. A clock that is far off breaks the activation handshake, so turn on automatic time and try again.

fixes.title: Flush DNS and try activating again
fixes.detail: In an elevated Command Prompt, run `ipconfig /flushdns` and then `slmgr /ato` to force an activation attempt. When you are on the corporate network and both DNS and the KMS host are working, activation succeeds right away.

fixes.title: Have IT check the KMS host
fixes.detail: Your IT team can make sure the KMS host service is running and that the _vlmcs._tcp DNS SRV record resolves. They can also point your PC at a specific host by running `slmgr /skms kmshost.yourdomain.com:1688` and then `slmgr /ato`.

fixes.title: Remove unauthorized activators and use a genuine license (personal PCs)
fixes.detail: A home PC should never activate through KMS. Uninstall any KMS activator software, run a full malware scan, and then activate with a genuine retail or digital license in Settings > System > Activation.
fixes.riskNote: KMS 'crack' tools often carry malware and break the license terms, so removing them fixes both a security problem and a compliance problem.

prevention: On managed devices, set the corporate VPN to connect before sign-in
For IT: keep an eye on KMS host health and the related DNS records
Keep the system clock synced with a reliable time source
Buy genuine licenses and never use activator tools

title: Boot selection failed: a required device is inaccessible
summary: Windows Boot Manager cannot reach the drive it needs to start Windows. Usually the Boot Configuration Data (BCD) is missing entries, or the disk or its controller is not available.
meaning: Status 0xc000000e means the boot loader went looking for the system volume and the device was not there. The BCD can lose track of the Windows partition after a disk swap, a switch between UEFI and Legacy mode in the BIOS, a failed update, or a sudden power loss. The PC then gets stuck in a boot repair loop or on a black screen.
commonCauses: Boot Configuration Data (BCD) entries that are missing or out of date
A changed BIOS boot order, or the wrong disk listed first
A SATA or NVMe drive that is not detected (loose cable or failing controller)
A boot partition damaged by a failed update or a power cut
Secure Boot or CSM settings changed during hardware work

fixes.title: Check boot order and whether the drive is detected
fixes.detail: Open firmware setup (usually F2, Del, or F12 right after power-on) and make sure the Windows disk is listed and set as the first boot device. If the disk is not listed at all, shut down and reseat its cable.

fixes.title: Run Startup Repair from recovery media
fixes.detail: Boot from a Windows installation USB and go to Repair your computer > Troubleshoot > Advanced options > Startup Repair. Let it try to repair the BCD automatically.

fixes.title: Rebuild the BCD by hand
fixes.detail: In Advanced options > Command Prompt, run `bootrec /fixmbr`, then `bootrec /fixboot`, then `bootrec /rebuildbcd`. When it finds your Windows installation, answer A to add it.
fixes.riskNote: These commands write to the disk's boot sector. Be sure you are working on the right disk, because targeting the wrong one can stop another operating system on the PC from booting.

fixes.title: Scan the file system with chkdsk
fixes.detail: In the recovery Command Prompt, run `chkdsk C: /f /r`, using whatever drive letter Windows actually has there if it is not C:. Damage to the file system on the boot volume is a common cause of this error.
fixes.riskNote: On a disk that is physically failing, chkdsk can push it into complete failure. Copy important data off first if you can.

fixes.title: Recreate the boot files with bcdboot
fixes.detail: If rebuildbcd does not find any installation, use `diskpart` to give the EFI partition a drive letter (select volume, then assign letter). Then run `bcdboot C:\Windows /s S: /f UEFI`, where S: is the letter you gave the EFI partition.
fixes.riskNote: diskpart and bcdboot write directly to partitions, and the wrong volume letter can wipe out another partition's boot files. Run `list volume` and double-check before writing anything.

prevention: Have a Windows installation USB ready before you change disks or BIOS settings
Do not force the PC off while an update is installing
After cloning or replacing a drive, update the BCD instead of assuming it carried over
On BitLocker-encrypted disks, have your recovery key on hand before attempting boot repairs

title: UNMOUNTABLE_BOOT_VOLUME
summary: Windows crashed during startup because it could not mount the file system on the boot volume. NTFS corruption or a failing boot drive is almost always the cause.
meaning: Stop code 0x000000ED appears during startup when the kernel asks NTFS to mount the system volume and the mount fails. Unclean shutdowns, disk corruption, and hardware faults on the boot drive are the usual triggers, and the crash happens on every boot until the volume is repaired.
commonCauses: NTFS file system corruption after the PC was not shut down cleanly
A hard drive or SSD that is failing and has unreadable sectors
A loose or damaged SATA data cable or power connector
A storage controller mode change in the BIOS (for example, switching between AHCI and IDE/RAID)
System files damaged by malware or by an update that failed

fixes.title: Fix the file system with chkdsk from recovery
fixes.detail: Boot from a Windows USB, or let startup fail twice so WinRE opens, then go to Command Prompt and run `chkdsk C: /f /r`. It repairs file system damage and flags bad sectors.
fixes.riskNote: On a disk that is physically failing, chkdsk's full read pass can finish it off. If the data matters, image or copy the disk first.

fixes.title: Check the storage mode in the BIOS
fixes.detail: Open firmware setup and make sure the SATA/NVMe controller is set to the same mode Windows was installed in, which is usually AHCI. A changed mode is a well-known cause of this stop code.

fixes.title: Reseat the cables and check the drive
fixes.detail: Shut down, reseat the drive's data and power cables (or the M.2 module), and boot again. To check drive health, use the manufacturer's SMART tool or run `wmic diskdrive get status` from the recovery Command Prompt.

fixes.title: Repair the boot files
fixes.detail: If chkdsk alone does not get Windows booting, run `bootrec /fixmbr`, `bootrec /fixboot`, and `bootrec /rebuildbcd` in the WinRE Command Prompt.
fixes.riskNote: bootrec writes to boot sectors. Make sure you are working on the right disk, especially if the PC dual-boots.

fixes.title: Restore or reinstall if the volume cannot be repaired
fixes.detail: From WinRE, use System Restore to go back to a restore point from when things worked. If the drive fails its SMART checks, replace it and reinstall Windows from the USB media.
fixes.riskNote: A new disk starts empty, so anything not backed up is gone. Check your backups before you reset or replace the drive.

prevention: Never cut power while an update is installing or the disk is writing
Check SMART health once a month (for example, the HealthStatus value from Get-PhysicalDisk)
Keep tested backups of the system drive
Replace SATA cables when you move or rebuild hardware

title: The application was unable to start correctly (0xc000007b)
summary: An app or game will not launch because of a 32-bit/64-bit DLL mismatch or damaged runtime libraries. It usually happens right after an install or a driver update.
meaning: 0xc000007b is STATUS_INVALID_IMAGE_FORMAT. Windows loaded an executable or DLL whose bitness or binary format did not match what the process expected. The textbook example is a 32-bit DLL loaded into a 64-bit program. In practice, damaged Visual C++ redistributables and GPU driver DLLs cause it most often.
commonCauses: Visual C++ redistributable runtimes that are damaged
32-bit and 64-bit DLLs mixed together in the program's folder
GPU driver DLLs that are corrupt or mismatched (common with games)
A broken app install or an update that did not finish
Disk corruption that damaged program files

fixes.title: Repair or reinstall the Visual C++ redistributables
fixes.detail: Go to Settings > Apps > Installed apps and repair every Microsoft Visual C++ Redistributable entry, both x86 and x64. Alternatively, download the latest redistributable installers from Microsoft and install both architectures.

fixes.title: Reinstall the app that fails
fixes.detail: Uninstall the program, restart the PC, and install it again from the original installer. This replaces any mixed 32-bit and 64-bit DLLs sitting in the app's own folder.

fixes.title: Run DISM and SFC
fixes.detail: Open Terminal (Admin) and run `DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth`, followed by `sfc /scannow`. Together they repair corrupted system runtime files.

fixes.title: Reinstall the GPU driver cleanly
fixes.detail: For games, remove the current GPU driver completely (many people use the third-party tool DDU in Safe Mode for this), then install the newest driver straight from NVIDIA, AMD, or Intel.
fixes.riskNote: The display will flicker and reset while the driver reinstalls. Use a stable connection and do not interrupt the installer.

fixes.title: Check the disk for corruption
fixes.detail: If several programs stopped working at the same time, run `chkdsk C: /f` and `sfc /scannow`. File system corruption can quietly damage many program files at once.

prevention: After a reinstall of Windows, install both the x86 and x64 VC++ redistributables
Get GPU drivers directly from the manufacturer instead of relying only on Windows Update
Do not copy DLLs from another computer into a program's folder

title: The application was unable to start correctly (0xc0000142)
summary: This is STATUS_DLL_INIT_FAILED. A DLL the program depends on could not initialize, so Windows ends the process before any window appears.
meaning: 0xc0000142 means a DLL's DllMain initialization routine failed, and Windows refused to start the process as a result. It can hit Office apps, games, and background services, and it usually shows up after a Windows update, a GPU driver change, or corruption in system files.
commonCauses: System DLLs damaged by an update or by disk problems
A GPU driver that is failing or incompatible (especially with games and 3D apps)
Damaged Visual C++ or .NET runtimes
A corrupt font cache that stops apps with a GUI from starting
A conflict with other software, which a clean boot will reveal

fixes.title: Run DISM and SFC
fixes.detail: In Terminal (Admin), run `DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth` and then `sfc /scannow`. This replaces corrupted system DLLs, which are the most frequent cause of this code.

fixes.title: Update or reinstall the GPU driver
fixes.detail: Download and install the newest driver from your graphics card maker's website. When a game fails with this code, a clean driver reinstall fixes it surprisingly often.

fixes.title: Repair the runtimes and the app
fixes.detail: Repair every Microsoft Visual C++ redistributable, then use the app's built-in repair. For Office, that is Settings > Apps > Modify > Online Repair.

fixes.title: Use a clean boot to find conflicts
fixes.detail: Open `msconfig`, pick Selective startup, and disable third-party services. Restart and try the app. If it works, turn half of the services back on at a time until you find the one causing the problem.
fixes.riskNote: Keep a list of the services you turn off so you can return to normal startup when you are done.

prevention: Let Windows updates finish completely instead of cancelling them
Install GPU drivers with the manufacturer's own installer
When an app starts acting up, repair it right away rather than ignoring it

title: Catastrophic failure (0x8000FFFF / E_UNEXPECTED)
summary: A very generic HRESULT that basically means 'something failed in a way the caller did not expect'. It shows up in Windows Update, System Restore, and the Microsoft Store.
meaning: 0x8000FFFF is E_UNEXPECTED. Unlike more specific codes, it does not tell you what went wrong. It appears whenever a component runs into a condition it was not written to handle. When you see it in Windows Update or System Restore, the real problem is usually the component store or the servicing stack.
commonCauses: A corrupt Windows component store (WinSxS)
A broken Windows Update servicing stack
Shadow copy storage for System Restore that is set up incorrectly
Third-party antivirus getting in the way of servicing
Running out of disk space during a servicing operation

fixes.title: Repair the component store
fixes.detail: In Terminal (Admin), run `DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth` and then `sfc /scannow`. Restart and try the action that failed again.

fixes.title: Reset the Windows Update components
fixes.detail: Stop the update services with `net stop wuauserv` and `net stop bits`, rename C:\Windows\SoftwareDistribution to SoftwareDistribution.old, and start the services again with `net start bits` and `net start wuauserv`.
fixes.riskNote: Any partly downloaded updates are thrown away and downloaded again. Do not stop halfway through the service steps.

fixes.title: Free up disk space and try again
fixes.detail: Make sure the system drive has at least 15-20 GB free, because servicing fails much more often when space is low. Storage Sense or Disk Cleanup can reclaim room.

fixes.title: Turn off third-party antivirus for a test
fixes.detail: Pause or uninstall any third-party security suite, retry the operation, and then turn protection back on. Real-time scanning hooks into servicing and can cause E_UNEXPECTED.
fixes.riskNote: Turn protection back on as soon as you finish testing so the PC is not left unprotected.

fixes.title: Check how System Restore is set up
fixes.detail: If the error comes from System Restore, run `vssadmin list shadows` in Terminal (Admin). Confirm that restore points exist and that shadow copy storage is configured, then try an older restore point.

prevention: Keep 15-20 GB of free space on the system drive
Pause your antivirus on purpose before large updates
If updates keep failing, run DISM and SFC from time to time

title: Windows Update installation failure (0x80070643 / ERROR_INSTALL_FAILURE)
summary: A cumulative update, a .NET update, or a Defender definition update fails partway through installing and reports a generic 'fatal error during installation'.
meaning: 0x80070643 is ERROR_INSTALL_FAILURE: the installer started but ended with a fatal error. It is one of the most common Windows Update codes. Usually it points to corruption in the component store, a .NET or Defender package that is blocked or in conflict, or leftover files in the SoftwareDistribution folder.
commonCauses: A corrupt Windows Update cache in SoftwareDistribution
Corruption in the component store (CBS)
A damaged .NET Framework install
Third-party antivirus or a boot configuration problem blocking servicing
Bad disk sectors under C:\Windows

fixes.title: Use the Windows Update troubleshooter
fixes.detail: Go to Settings > System > Troubleshoot > Other troubleshooters, find Windows Update, and select Run. It resets the update services and clears the cache for you.

fixes.title: Clear the update cache
fixes.detail: In Terminal (Admin), run `net stop wuauserv` and `net stop bits`. Rename C:\Windows\SoftwareDistribution to SoftwareDistribution.old, run `net start bits` and `net start wuauserv`, and then check for updates again.

fixes.title: Repair the component store
fixes.detail: Run `DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth` and then `sfc /scannow`. Restart, then try the update again.

fixes.title: Repair the .NET Framework
fixes.detail: If the failing update is for .NET, download the Microsoft .NET Framework Repair Tool, run it, and then install the update again.

fixes.title: Install the update yourself from the Microsoft Update Catalog
fixes.detail: Write down the KB number of the failed update, search for it in the Microsoft Update Catalog, download the .msu file, and run it. That skips the Windows Update pipeline that keeps failing.

prevention: Let updates finish installing without interruption
Keep the system drive healthy by running chkdsk now and then
Repair .NET as soon as Windows reports a problem with it

title: Update timeout (0x800705B4 / ERROR_TIMEOUT)
summary: An update task, usually checking for or downloading updates, hit its internal time limit and gave up. It is often a one-time problem but can also point to a proxy or network issue.
meaning: 0x800705B4 is ERROR_TIMEOUT (1460). Windows Update waits for a reply from the update service or the network and stops waiting if nothing comes back in time. You usually see it on unreliable connections, behind managed proxies, or when the update service itself is stuck.
commonCauses: An internet connection that is slow or drops during the download
A corporate proxy or VPN interfering with update traffic
The Windows Update service stuck in a bad state
Temporary overload on Microsoft's update servers
A firewall that is blocking the update endpoints

fixes.title: Restart and try again, since it is often temporary
fixes.detail: Restart the PC, make sure your network connection is stable, and check for updates again. A one-off timeout often goes away on the next try.

fixes.title: Use the Windows Update troubleshooter
fixes.detail: Go to Settings > System > Troubleshoot > Other troubleshooters, find Windows Update, and select Run.

fixes.title: Skip the VPN or proxy and flush DNS
fixes.detail: Disconnect from the VPN and turn off the proxy for now. Then run `ipconfig /flushdns` and try the update again.

fixes.title: Reset the update services
fixes.detail: Run `net stop wuauserv` and `net stop bits`, rename the SoftwareDistribution folder to SoftwareDistribution.old, start both services again with `net start bits` and `net start wuauserv`, and check for updates.

fixes.title: Confirm the update services are not disabled
fixes.detail: Open `services.msc` and check that Windows Update, BITS, and Cryptographic Services are not set to Disabled. If a tweaking tool switched them off, set them back to Manual or Automatic.

prevention: Do not install updates over an unstable or metered connection
Allow Microsoft's update endpoints through proxy and firewall rules
Keep the update services enabled, because 'update blocker' tools cause this error

title: Not enough memory or system resources (0x8007000E / ERROR_OUTOFMEMORY)
summary: Something on your PC asked Windows for memory and was turned down, producing the 'Out of memory or system resources' message. The cause may be RAM that is truly used up, or a single process that keeps leaking memory.
meaning: The code 0x8007000E maps to ERROR_OUTOFMEMORY. Windows declined a memory request because the commit limit (physical RAM plus the page file) or the paged pool had nothing left to give. You can see it in games, ordinary applications and even explorer.exe. On an 8 GB PC juggling many programs, the pressure is usually real; on a PC with plenty of RAM, a leak is the more likely explanation.
commonCauses: A process that leaks memory and slowly grows its commit charge
Not enough installed RAM for what you are asking the PC to do
A page file that has been turned off or set too small
Dozens of browser tabs, Electron-based apps or virtual machines open at once
Defective RAM or memory corruption
Malware such as a hidden cryptominer quietly consuming resources

fixes.title: Find the process eating memory in Task Manager
fixes.detail: Open Task Manager with Ctrl+Shift+Esc, go to the Details tab, right-click a column header to add 'Commit size', then sort by that column. End or restart whatever is at the top if it keeps growing. If browser tabs are the repeat offender, a tab-sleeping extension or the browser's built-in sleeping tabs feature helps.

fixes.title: Reboot the PC
fixes.detail: Restarting clears out committed memory and the paged pool in one step. When the system is simply overloaded, nothing gives relief faster.

fixes.title: Turn the page file back on or give it a sensible size
fixes.detail: Run `sysdm.cpl`, then open Advanced > Performance Settings > Advanced > Virtual memory > Change. The simplest choice is 'Automatically manage paging file size for all drives'. If someone had disabled it, a custom initial size of about 1.5 times your installed RAM is a reasonable starting point.
fixes.riskNote: Running with no page file at all causes memory-hungry programs to fail sooner and can prevent Windows from writing crash dumps.

fixes.title: Check the RAM for hardware faults
fixes.detail: Launch `mdsched.exe` (Windows Memory Diagnostic) and let it restart and test. Afterward, open Event Viewer and look for the MemoryDiagnostics-Results entry to confirm whether a module is failing.

fixes.title: Run a malware scan
fixes.detail: Start a Full scan in Windows Security. Cryptominers and botnet software are frequent, well-hidden consumers of memory.

prevention: Size your RAM to your workload, and plan an upgrade if commit usage regularly sits above 90%
Leave the page file set to system-managed
Track the 'Committed' figure in Task Manager's Memory panel instead of only the RAM percentage

title: 0x80070490 / ERROR_NOT_FOUND: Element not found
summary: During setup or servicing, a Windows component went looking for a package, file or registry value that is not there. You typically see it during feature updates, Microsoft Defender updates or attempts to repair the component store.
meaning: The value 0x80070490 corresponds to ERROR_NOT_FOUND (Win32 error 1160), whose message is 'Element not found'. Practically speaking, the servicing stack expected to find a component in the component store and it was missing or did not match, or a registry or policy value the calling program depends on has been removed.
commonCauses: A damaged or partially populated component store
Registry values stripped out by aggressive 'debloat' tools
A servicing stack left broken by an update that failed
Third-party cleaner apps removing keys Windows still needs
Corrupted CBS manifest files

fixes.title: Fix the component store with DISM and SFC
fixes.detail: Open Terminal (Admin) and run `DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth`. It downloads replacement files, so make sure the internet connection works. When it finishes, run `sfc /scannow`, restart the PC and try the update again.

fixes.title: Use the Windows Update troubleshooter
fixes.detail: Go to Settings > System > Troubleshoot > Other troubleshooters, click Run next to Windows Update, and then retry the installation.

fixes.title: Undo the effects of 'debloat' or cleaner utilities
fixes.detail: Did you recently run a registry cleaner or a debloat script? If so, it is the most probable cause. Use System Restore to return to a restore point made before that tool ran, and stop using it going forward.
fixes.riskNote: System Restore reverts drivers and registry settings. Save open work and jot down anything you installed recently before you begin.

fixes.title: Fall back to an in-place upgrade
fixes.detail: Get the Windows 11 or Windows 10 ISO from Microsoft, mount it, launch setup.exe and select 'Keep personal files and apps'. Setup rebuilds the component store on top of your existing installation, and your data stays put.
fixes.riskNote: Make a backup of your personal files first. An in-place upgrade can sometimes reset default apps and some drivers.

prevention: Keep registry cleaners and debloat scripts away from the servicing stack
Install updates soon after release so the component store does not fall out of step
Create a restore point before running any tool that changes system settings

title: Code 45: hardware device is not connected (CM_PROB_PHANTOM)
summary: In Device Manager you see 'Currently, this hardware device is not connected to the computer. (Code 45)'. Windows remembers the device and has a driver for it, but cannot reach it right now.
meaning: Code 45 is one of Device Manager's problem codes. It tells you Windows knows the device (there is a driver and a history entry), yet the hardware is not showing up on its bus at the moment. With a removable device, that usually just means it is unplugged. With built-in hardware such as a webcam, Wi-Fi card or Bluetooth adapter, it can point to a loose connector, hardware that has been powered down, or a component that has died.
commonCauses: The external device is unplugged, or its cable or port has failed
USB selective suspend or another power-saving feature switching the port off
An internal device turned off in the BIOS/UEFI, or a connector that has worked loose
An outdated device entry lingering after a driver update
A USB hub or docking station that is failing

fixes.title: Plug into a different port, without a hub
fixes.detail: Connect the device straight to one of the USB ports on the back of the PC (the ones on the motherboard), bypassing hubs and front-panel ports. If the cable is removable, swap in a different one too.

fixes.title: Have Windows rescan the hardware
fixes.detail: Open Device Manager and choose Action > Scan for hardware changes. Alternatively, restart the PC with the device plugged in so Windows enumerates it from scratch.

fixes.title: Turn off USB power saving
fixes.detail: In Device Manager, expand Universal Serial Bus controllers, open each USB Root Hub or Generic USB Hub, and on the Power Management tab clear 'Allow the computer to turn off this device to save power'. Then unplug and reconnect the device.

fixes.title: Remove the device so Windows sets it up again
fixes.detail: Right-click the device showing Code 45, pick Uninstall device, and then run Action > Scan for hardware changes. Windows creates a fresh device entry using the current driver.

fixes.title: Inspect firmware settings and internal cables
fixes.detail: For built-in hardware such as a webcam, card reader or Bluetooth module, open the BIOS/UEFI setup and make sure the device is enabled. On a desktop, also confirm its internal cable is firmly seated.
fixes.riskNote: Shut the PC down and unplug it from the wall before you reseat any internal cable.

prevention: Connect devices that stay plugged in permanently to the rear motherboard ports
Keep your chipset and USB drivers up to date
Install firmware updates for your dock, since they often cure repeated connect and disconnect cycles

title: STATUS_SYSTEM_PROCESS_TERMINATED (0xC000021A)
summary: One of the essential user-mode processes, WinLogon or the Client Server Run-Time Subsystem (CSRSS), quit without warning, and Windows halts with stop code 0xC000021A.
meaning: Windows treats WinLogon and CSRSS as indispensable: if either one stops, the entire session falls apart. So when one of them ends unexpectedly, the kernel has no way to carry on and raises bug check 0xC000021A. You will nearly always meet this error during startup or sign-in, and it often follows a Windows update, the installation of third-party security software, or a power cut in the middle of a shutdown.
commonCauses: System files left damaged or out of sync by a Windows update that was interrupted or only partly applied
Third-party antivirus or endpoint protection hooking into the sign-in processes
Corrupted WinLogon or CSRSS executables on disk
A failing drive that drops writes to system files

fixes.title: Run Startup Repair from WinRE
fixes.detail: Interrupt the boot three times in a row (power off as Windows starts loading) to bring up the Windows Recovery Environment. Then go to Troubleshoot > Advanced options > Startup Repair. It can undo the incomplete operation that left WinLogon or CSRSS broken.

fixes.title: Remove the most recent quality update
fixes.detail: Inside WinRE, open Troubleshoot > Advanced options > Uninstall Updates and pick 'Uninstall latest quality update'. This backs out the patch that is often behind a WinLogon failure on a 0xC000021A boot.

fixes.title: Repair the offline installation with DISM and SFC
fixes.detail: Open Command Prompt in WinRE and run `dism /image:C:\ /cleanup-image /restorehealth`, then `sfc /scannow /offbootdir=C:\ /offwindir=C:\Windows`. If Windows lives on a different drive letter in WinRE, substitute it. Both tools repair damaged system files without Windows needing to boot.

fixes.title: Scan the system drive for errors
fixes.detail: In that same WinRE prompt, run `chkdsk C: /f /r`. Writes to system files that were lost or delayed are a known trigger for 0xC000021A, and chkdsk fixes the resulting file-system damage.
fixes.riskNote: Let chkdsk run to completion. On a failing drive, it may take several hours.

fixes.title: Final options: System Restore or Reset this PC
fixes.detail: Start with System Restore and choose a point from before the crashes began. If no restore point exists, use Reset this PC from WinRE and select Keep my files. A clean install is what remains if both fail.
fixes.riskNote: A reset preserves personal files but uninstalls your apps, so back up beforehand.

prevention: Make a fresh System Restore point before installing antivirus or system utilities
Never switch the PC off while it shows 'Working on updates'; let updates finish
Keep an eye on drive health with `wmic diskdrive get status` or a tool such as CrystalDiskInfo

title: STATUS_STACK_BUFFER_OVERRUN (0xC0000409)
summary: Windows caught a stack buffer overrun, or a program intentionally invoked __fastfail, and shut the process down on the spot. If that process is a protected one, the whole system bug checks with 0xC0000409.
meaning: Microsoft builds modern Windows components with /GS stack cookies and Control Flow Guard. When a stack cookie gets overwritten, or code calls __fastfail, Windows ends the offending process instantly. If the process sits close to the kernel or is a protected system process, you get a blue screen with 0xC0000409 instead of a single app crash. On Windows 11 this is also a textbook symptom of an unstable memory overclock (XMP or EXPO).
commonCauses: An XMP/EXPO memory overclock that is not fully stable, corrupting stack cookies
A defective RAM stick
A kernel-mode driver that is buggy or out of date and overwrites memory
Security software, or corrupted system binaries, triggering a fastfail

fixes.title: Test memory with Windows Memory Diagnostic
fixes.detail: Press `Win+R`, type `mdsched.exe`, and choose 'Restart now and check for problems'. Allow the test to complete, then open Event Viewer (Windows Logs > System) and find the entry from source MemoryDiagnostics-Results.

fixes.title: Disable XMP/EXPO overclocking
fixes.detail: Open the UEFI/BIOS setup and return the memory to its default JEDEC speed by turning off XMP or EXPO. If the blue screens stop, either run the profile at a lower speed or install a newer BIOS that improves memory stability.
fixes.riskNote: Stick to the memory settings. Leave voltage options alone unless you know exactly what they do.

fixes.title: Update graphics, chipset and storage drivers
fixes.detail: Get the newest GPU driver from NVIDIA, AMD or Intel, and the chipset drivers from your motherboard or PC maker. Faulty kernel drivers are the top cause of this error when hardware is not to blame.

fixes.title: Fix system files using DISM and SFC
fixes.detail: In Terminal (Admin), run `dism /online /cleanup-image /restorehealth` and then `sfc /scannow`. Damaged protected binaries can cause fastfail terminations.

fixes.title: Uninstall third-party antivirus for a trial period
fixes.detail: Take off any non-Microsoft antivirus or endpoint software for about a week; Microsoft Defender switches on automatically to keep you protected. If the crashes go away, ask the vendor for a corrected version.

prevention: Run a complete memtest86 pass on any memory overclock before using it every day
Keep the BIOS, chipset drivers and GPU drivers current
Stay away from beta drivers on a machine you rely on for work

title: 0xC0000098: WINLOAD.EFI is missing or corrupt
summary: Windows Boot Manager cannot load winload.efi (or, in some cases, the system registry hive) because the file is absent or damaged, so startup stops with error 0xC0000098.
meaning: With 0xC0000098, the boot manager located the boot entry, but the file that entry points to cannot be read or is not valid. The screen usually reads something like 'File: \Windows\system32\winload.efi' with 'Status: 0xc0000098'. It tends to show up after an update fails, after disk corruption, after an antivirus product 'cleans' a boot file, or after a disk was cloned onto a different partition layout.
commonCauses: winload.efi damaged or quarantined, frequently by third-party antivirus
BCD entries that reference the wrong partition or identifier
File-system corruption caused by a power cut or an interrupted update
A disk clone or partition resize that relocated the boot files

fixes.title: Rebuild the BCD in WinRE
fixes.detail: Boot from Windows installation media or force WinRE to load, open Command Prompt, and run `bootrec /rebuildbcd` followed by `bootrec /fixboot`. If fixboot returns 'Access is denied', mount the EFI partition as S: and run `bcdboot C:\Windows /s S: /f UEFI` instead.
fixes.riskNote: These commands rewrite boot configuration. Confirm which drive letter Windows has in WinRE before you start.

fixes.title: Restore the SYSTEM hive when it is the file named
fixes.detail: If the error lists \Windows\system32\config\system instead of winload.efi, run `copy C:\Windows\System32\config\RegBack\system C:\Windows\System32\config\` from WinRE. On recent builds the RegBack folder is often empty; in that case, go with System Restore.
fixes.riskNote: You are replacing a core registry file. Copy the damaged hive to another name first so you can put it back.

fixes.title: Check the Windows volume with chkdsk
fixes.detail: In the WinRE Command Prompt, run `chkdsk C: /f /r`. This repairs any file-system damage affecting winload.efi. Restart afterward and see whether Windows loads.

fixes.title: Roll back with System Restore in WinRE
fixes.detail: Go to Troubleshoot > Advanced options > System Restore and select a restore point dated before the first failed startup. Boot files and the BCD state come back together.

prevention: Create a restore point before running antivirus scans that reach into system folders
Add the boot files to your third-party antivirus exclusion list
Keep a Windows 11 installation USB drive available for offline repairs

title: STATUS_CANNOT_LOAD_REGISTRY_HIVE (0xC0000218)
summary: Windows stops during startup with 0xC0000218 because a registry hive, most often SOFTWARE or SYSTEM, is damaged and will not load.
meaning: Early in the boot process the kernel loads the SYSTEM and SOFTWARE registry hives. Should one of them fail its integrity checks (for example, because power was lost mid-write, the disk is damaged, or a disk-imaging tool crashed), the kernel bug checks with 0xC0000218. The screen usually tells you which hive file failed.
commonCauses: A power cut or forced shutdown while the registry was being written
An SSD or hard drive that is failing and losing writes
Disk-imaging or 'cleaner' tools damaging hive files
File-system corruption left by an update that was interrupted

fixes.title: Copy back the hive from RegBack
fixes.detail: In the WinRE Command Prompt, run `dir C:\Windows\System32\config\RegBack`. If the SYSTEM and SOFTWARE files there are larger than zero bytes, copy them into C:\Windows\System32\config\. Windows 10 and 11 frequently leave RegBack empty, and in that case System Restore is the better route.
fixes.riskNote: Before overwriting, rename the damaged hive with a .bak extension so the original is preserved.

fixes.title: Run chkdsk before working on the hive
fixes.detail: From WinRE, run `chkdsk C: /f /r`. If the volume itself was damaged, repairing it may be enough to let the hive load. If not, at least the copy step that follows happens on a healthy file system.

fixes.title: Restore an earlier state with System Restore
fixes.detail: Choose Troubleshoot > Advanced options > System Restore and select a point from before the crash. The previous hive files are restored as a set, which makes this the tidiest solution whenever a restore point is available.

fixes.title: Reset this PC with Keep my files, or reinstall
fixes.detail: When there is neither a restore point nor a usable RegBack copy, open Reset this PC in WinRE and pick Keep my files. Your C:\Users folder is kept while Windows and its registry hives are rebuilt. A clean install is the last fallback.
fixes.riskNote: Installed apps are removed. If you can, copy any critical files out of your user profile first.

prevention: Protect against write-interrupting power loss with a UPS on desktops, or keep laptop batteries healthy
Schedule a weekly restore point with Task Scheduler
Stop running registry cleaner utilities

title: REFERENCE_BY_POINTER (0x00000018)
summary: The reference count on a kernel object went wrong, typically because it was released without a matching acquire, and Windows stops with REFERENCE_BY_POINTER.
meaning: The Windows kernel decides when to free an object by counting references to it. REFERENCE_BY_POINTER is raised when some code releases a reference it never took: either the count reaches zero too soon and the object is freed while something is still using it, or the count drops below zero. This is almost always a driver defect, and the blue screen often names the responsible driver, commonly a graphics, network or antivirus filter driver.
commonCauses: A kernel-mode driver that mishandles object references
A graphics or network driver left outdated after a Windows update
Filter drivers installed by antivirus or VPN software
Bad RAM flipping bits inside object headers

fixes.title: Bring graphics, network and storage drivers up to date
fixes.detail: Install the latest graphics driver from the GPU vendor, and get network and NVMe/RAID drivers from your PC or motherboard manufacturer. If the blue screen names a file (for example nvlddmkm.sys or tcpip.sys), start with the driver that file belongs to.

fixes.title: Roll back a driver that was just updated
fixes.detail: If the crashes began right after a driver update, open Device Manager, open the device, go to the Driver tab and choose Roll Back Driver (when the option is available). A newly delivered driver that immediately triggers REFERENCE_BY_POINTER is usually the one at fault.

fixes.title: Test RAM with Windows Memory Diagnostic
fixes.detail: Run `mdsched.exe` and allow the PC to restart into the test. Reference counts stored in faulty memory are a known cause of this stop code.

fixes.title: Remove antivirus and VPN filter drivers for a while
fixes.detail: Uninstall any third-party antivirus and VPN software for a few days; Microsoft Defender remains on. Their kernel filter drivers are common culprits. Reinstall them one by one to find which one causes trouble.

fixes.title: Use Driver Verifier and dump analysis if crashes continue
fixes.detail: Run `verifier`, choose standard settings, and select all non-Microsoft drivers. Let the crash happen once, then examine the resulting memory dump yourself or share it on a support forum. Turn Driver Verifier off afterward with `verifier /reset`.
fixes.riskNote: Driver Verifier is designed to crash the system when it catches a bad driver. Save your work, and be ready for boot loops until you reset it (from Safe Mode if needed).

prevention: After a major Windows upgrade, update your drivers before putting the PC under heavy use
Check newly installed RAM with memtest86 before depending on it
Run only one antivirus product at a time

title: APC_INDEX_MISMATCH (0x00000001)
summary: APC_INDEX_MISMATCH means a kernel thread finished with its asynchronous procedure call (APC) state out of balance. A faulty driver is nearly always responsible.
meaning: Every kernel thread keeps track of its APC state with a pair of counters. When a driver turns APCs off and then fails to turn them back on in the right order (for instance calling KeEnterCriticalRegion without the matching KeLeaveCriticalRegion), Windows spots the imbalance when the thread returns and raises bug check 0x1. In practice the cases concentrate around printing components, older antivirus drivers and resource leaks in third-party kernel drivers.
commonCauses: A third-party kernel driver that does not pair its APC calls correctly (printer, antivirus or VPN drivers are typical)
Printer drivers that became corrupted during a driver update
A problem driver loaded at startup that interacts with win32k
Failing RAM, in rare cases

fixes.title: Write down the driver named on the blue screen
fixes.detail: The stop screen usually lists a .sys file, such as win32kbase.sys alongside a third-party driver. Look that file name up: the cure is to update or uninstall that particular driver, not to reinstall Windows.

fixes.title: Remove and reinstall your printer drivers
fixes.detail: Remove the printer under Settings > Bluetooth & devices > Printers & scanners (or in Print Management). Then open Print server properties, go to the Drivers tab and delete its driver package. Finish by installing the vendor's latest package. Printer drivers are the classic source of APC_INDEX_MISMATCH.

fixes.title: Update or roll back drivers you added recently
fixes.detail: If the blue screens started after you installed a VPN, antivirus or peripheral driver, update it to the newest version, or roll it back in Device Manager on the Driver tab with Roll Back Driver.

fixes.title: Repair Windows files if a Microsoft driver is named
fixes.detail: When the file listed belongs to Microsoft (win32k.sys, for example), open an admin terminal, run `dism /online /cleanup-image /restorehealth`, and then run `sfc /scannow` to repair system binaries.

prevention: Install current, vendor-signed drivers, printers above all
When switching security products, fully uninstall the old one before installing the new one
Download printer software from the manufacturer instead of third-party driver sites

title: THREAD_STUCK_IN_DEVICE_DRIVER (0x000000EA)
summary: A thread inside a device driver kept spinning for too long without finishing (the classic case is a graphics driver stuck in a loop), so Windows bug checks with THREAD_STUCK_IN_DEVICE_DRIVER.
meaning: Sometimes a driver's worker thread, almost always one belonging to the display driver, sits in a loop waiting for the hardware to report it is done, and that signal never comes. After a timeout, the kernel stops the system with THREAD_STUCK_IN_DEVICE_DRIVER. The responsible driver is shown on the stop screen (atikmdag.sys, amdkmdag.sys or nvlddmkm.sys, for example). Common triggers include 3D games, video playback and setups with several monitors.
commonCauses: A GPU that crashes or overheats, leaving its driver deadlocked
A graphics driver that is outdated or corrupted
A GPU overclock that is not stable, or power delivery that falls short
Failing graphics hardware or VRAM

fixes.title: Do a clean graphics driver reinstall with DDU
fixes.detail: Download Display Driver Uninstaller (DDU), restart into Safe Mode, and use it to strip out the current GPU driver. Then install the latest WHQL driver from NVIDIA, AMD or Intel. This clears out leftover driver state that a normal upgrade leaves in place.
fixes.riskNote: Once DDU removes the display driver, the screen runs at a low resolution until the new driver is installed.

fixes.title: Return the GPU to stock clocks
fixes.detail: Undo any core or memory overclock applied in MSI Afterburner or the BIOS, then test. If the system stays stable at stock settings, the card or its memory was being run past its limits.

fixes.title: Watch GPU temperatures and case airflow
fixes.detail: Use HWiNFO64 to monitor the GPU while it is under load. Temperatures that stay above roughly 90 °C mean the cooling needs attention: clear out dust, replace the thermal paste or improve airflow before you blame the driver.

fixes.title: Check power cables and PSU capacity
fixes.detail: Reseat the PCIe power cables, running separate cables from the power supply instead of one daisy-chained cable, and make sure the PSU wattage meets the graphics card's requirement. Insufficient power causes exactly this freeze-then-crash pattern.
fixes.riskNote: Turn the PC off and unplug it before handling internal cables.

fixes.title: Stress-test the GPU and replace it if it fails at stock
fixes.detail: Run a sustained load at stock clocks, such as 20 minutes of FurMark or a demanding game. If it still crashes after a clean driver install, the hardware is probably failing. Testing the card in another PC, if you can, confirms it.

prevention: Stick with current WHQL GPU drivers, and avoid beta releases on work PCs
Look after GPU cooling, and clean dust filters about twice a year
Do not pair an overclocked GPU with a power supply that is already borderline

title: VIDEO_DXGKRNL_FATAL_ERROR (0x113)
summary: The DirectX graphics kernel detected a fatal violation by the display driver, and Windows stops with VIDEO_DXGKRNL_FATAL_ERROR.
meaning: dxgkrnl.sys, the DirectX Graphics Kernel, sits between Windows and your GPU driver and enforces the rules. When the display driver cannot recover after a timeout detection and recovery (TDR) event, or breaks the DirectX driver model, the graphics kernel brings the system down. It usually happens while gaming, during video calls or when HDR or display scaling settings change, and its root causes overlap heavily with VIDEO_TDR_FAILURE.
commonCauses: A GPU driver (NVIDIA, AMD or Intel) that is unstable or out of date
A GPU that runs too hot or is unstable even at factory settings
A display driver that no longer matches Windows after an upgrade
A power supply that cannot sustain the GPU's boost clocks

fixes.title: Reinstall the GPU driver cleanly with DDU
fixes.detail: Run Display Driver Uninstaller in Safe Mode, then install the newest WHQL driver from your GPU maker. On laptops, install the manufacturer's chipset package as well. This step fixes most cases of this error.

fixes.title: Turn off GPU overclocks, factory OC modes included
fixes.detail: Put Afterburner or BIOS overclocks back to stock. Some cards ship with a factory 'OC mode' that is only marginally stable, so switch to reference clocks and test for a week.

fixes.title: Install the latest BIOS and chipset drivers
fixes.detail: Motherboard makers often include PCIe and Resizable BAR stability fixes in BIOS releases. Update the BIOS and chipset drivers, particularly if you put a new graphics card into an older board.
fixes.riskNote: Follow the manufacturer's BIOS update steps to the letter, and never cut power while the flash is in progress.

fixes.title: Check temperatures and power delivery
fixes.detail: Record GPU temperature, hotspot temperature and clock speeds under load with HWiNFO64. Thermal throttling and power drops lead to repeated dxgkrnl crashes, so clean the cooler and reseat the power cables.

fixes.title: Try the GPU in another slot or PC if crashes persist
fixes.detail: If the error continues at stock clocks with a freshly installed driver, hardware becomes the prime suspect. Move the card to a second PCIe slot (if it is usable) or test it in another computer to isolate the problem.
fixes.riskNote: Power the PC off before you reseat any hardware.

prevention: Update your GPU driver at least once a quarter
Keep GPU fans free of dust, and check hotspot temperatures as the seasons change
Pick a power supply whose quality and wattage suit your graphics card's generation

title: ERROR_INVALID_PARAMETER (0x80070057)
summary: A Windows component received a value it refuses to accept. Error 0x80070057 appears in Windows Update, OneDrive, Microsoft Store installs, backups and user profile tasks.
meaning: 0x80070057 is the HRESULT form of Win32 error 87, ERROR_INVALID_PARAMETER, which means a program handed a system API an argument that the API rejected. Because the code is so general, the real cause depends on where you saw it: a corrupted SoftwareDistribution folder for Windows Update, a damaged user profile, broken OneDrive sync metadata, or a backup or restore tool calling APIs the wrong way. The fix usually involves repairing whatever state the failing component has corrupted, not hunting for a single setting.
commonCauses: Corrupted Windows Update components (the SoftwareDistribution and Catroot2 folders)
A damaged user profile or corrupted component-store metadata
Third-party backup or sync tools sending invalid parameters
Storage or filter drivers interfering with file operations

fixes.title: Reset Windows Update components
fixes.detail: Open an admin terminal and run `net stop wuauserv` and `net stop bits`. Rename `C:\Windows\SoftwareDistribution` to `SoftwareDistribution.old` and rename `C:\Windows\System32\catroot2` to `catroot2.old`. Then run `net start bits` and `net start wuauserv`, and try the update once more.
fixes.riskNote: Renaming does not delete anything, and Windows recreates both folders automatically. If catroot2 will not rename, also stop the cryptsvc service first.

fixes.title: Repair with DISM and SFC
fixes.detail: In an admin terminal, run `dism /online /cleanup-image /restorehealth`, followed by `sfc /scannow`. These repair the component store that the update installer relies on, which is the most frequent fix for 0x80070057.

fixes.title: Try the Windows Update troubleshooter
fixes.detail: Open Settings > System > Troubleshoot > Other troubleshooters and click Run beside Windows Update. It resets service registrations and settings automatically, which often clears the invalid-parameter condition.

fixes.title: Test in a new local user account
fixes.detail: If the error happens with Store, OneDrive or profile-related actions, add a new local account (Settings > Accounts > Other users) and repeat the task there. If it works, the original profile is corrupted, and moving your data to the new account is better than trying to patch the old one.

fixes.title: Temporarily pause third-party backup and security software
fixes.detail: Turn off backup, sync or security suites while you repeat the failing operation. Filter drivers that intercept file I/O are a known cause of invalid-parameter errors.

prevention: Keep Windows Update healthy by never cutting power during an installation
Use just one sync or backup tool for each set of data so filter drivers do not collide
Run DISM every few months as routine maintenance

title: ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED (0x80070005)
summary: The caller was refused access to a resource. Error 0x80070005 turns up in Windows Update, Microsoft Store installs, COM and WMI operations, services and network shares whenever permissions or policies get in the way.
meaning: 0x80070005 is the HRESULT version of Win32 error 5, ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED. Whatever made the request (an app, a service or the Windows Update agent) did not have the permission the target demands. Where you see it tells you how to fix it: an Update failure suggests broken file or registry ACLs on Update components, a Store install failure points to the WindowsApps folder, and scripts that fail against WMI or COM suggest DCOM launch permissions or antivirus interference.
commonCauses: Damaged permissions on system folders or registry keys, often after 'tweak' tools
Antivirus or Controlled Folder Access blocking legitimate writes
Scripts or scheduled tasks running without administrator elevation
Corrupted Windows Update components or Microsoft Store cache

fixes.title: Try again with administrator rights
