Most of the time the service has been disabled, whether by hand, by an 'optimizer' utility, by malware, or by a third-party antivirus that did not hand control back cleanly. The other common cause is a broken WMI, which the service relies on.
commonCauses: The Security Center (wscsvc) service is set to Disabled or will not leave the stopped state
Problems with the WMI service or its repository leave Security Center without data
Remnants of a third-party antivirus that unregistered Defender but never returned status reporting
Malware that intentionally switched the service off

fixes.title: Start the Security Center service
fixes.detail: Press Win+R, run `services.msc`, and locate 'Security Center'. Set its Startup type to 'Automatic (Delayed Start)' and click Start. Then open Windows Security again to see whether the banner has cleared.

fixes.title: Restart Windows Management Instrumentation
fixes.detail: In `services.msc`, right-click 'Windows Management Instrumentation' and choose Restart (services that depend on it restart too), then start Security Center once more. A hung WMI is a frequent hidden cause when Security Center appears to start but the app still shows it as off.
fixes.riskNote: Restarting WMI briefly disrupts management and monitoring tools that rely on it, so avoid doing it during backups or remote management sessions.

fixes.title: Completely remove any conflicting third-party antivirus
fixes.detail: Uninstall third-party antivirus software from Settings → Apps, then run the vendor's dedicated removal tool to clean up what remains. Leftover antivirus registrations are the classic reason Security Center cannot build a complete protection status.

fixes.title: Repair system files using DISM and SFC
fixes.detail: Open Command Prompt as administrator and run `DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth` followed by `sfc /scannow`. This fixes damaged security components that the services rely on. Restart when both finish.

fixes.title: Check the PC for malware
fixes.detail: Go to Windows Security → Virus & threat protection → Scan options and run a 'Full scan', or choose 'Microsoft Defender Offline scan' for threats that keep coming back. Malware often disables Security Center, so confirm the system is clean before treating the issue as solved.

prevention: Run a single active antivirus product, and use the vendor's cleanup tool whenever you uninstall one
Stay away from 'optimizer' and 'debloat' tools that switch off security services
Leave Defender platform and security intelligence updates turned on

title: This PC can't run Windows 11: The PC must support TPM 2.0
codes: This PC must support Secure Boot
summary: Windows 11 Setup or the PC Health Check app tells you "This PC can't run Windows 11" and "The PC must support TPM 2.0," often with a Secure Boot warning as well. The computer does not meet the hardware security requirements for Windows 11, so the installer will not continue.
meaning: Windows 11 needs a TPM 2.0 module, UEFI firmware that is Secure Boot capable, and a processor from a supported generation. This message is not a sign that Windows is damaged. The installer is stopping the upgrade because one of those requirements is missing or turned off. Quite often the PC already has TPM 2.0 built into the processor (Intel PTT or AMD fTPM), and it is just disabled in the firmware. Turning it on is enough to pass the check.
commonCauses: The firmware TPM (Intel PTT or AMD fTPM) is switched off in BIOS/UEFI setup
The PC boots in Legacy/CSM mode instead of UEFI, and Secure Boot is off
The system disk uses MBR partitioning, while UEFI boot needs GPT
The processor or its generation is truly not supported by Windows 11

fixes.title: Find out exactly which requirement fails
fixes.detail: Press Win+R and run `tpm.msc` to see whether a TPM exists and reports 'The TPM is ready for use'. Run `msinfo32` and look at 'BIOS Mode' (UEFI or Legacy) and 'Secure Boot State'. Then run PC Health Check again for the complete list of unmet requirements before you change any settings.

fixes.title: Turn on the firmware TPM (Intel PTT or AMD fTPM)
fixes.detail: Open firmware setup by pressing F2 or Del at the startup logo, then look in the Security or Advanced section. Enable 'Intel Platform Trust Technology (PTT)' on Intel systems or 'fTPM' on AMD systems, save, and boot into Windows. Run `tpm.msc` again to confirm TPM 2.0 is ready.

fixes.title: Move to UEFI boot and turn on Secure Boot
fixes.detail: If `msinfo32` reports Legacy BIOS mode, back up your files first. In an elevated Command Prompt, check the disk with `mbr2gpt.exe /validate /allowFullOS` and then convert it with `mbr2gpt.exe /convert /allowFullOS`. Once that succeeds, set the firmware to UEFI mode, enable Secure Boot, and check the requirements again.
fixes.riskNote: mbr2gpt rewrites the partition table of the Windows disk, and a failed conversion can leave the PC unable to boot. Make a backup first, target only the operating system disk, and never run it on data disks.

fixes.title: Update the BIOS or firmware
fixes.detail: On some motherboards, the TPM, PTT, fTPM and Secure Boot options only appear after a firmware update. Get the newest BIOS from your motherboard or laptop maker's support site, install it, and then review the firmware settings again.
fixes.riskNote: Do not interrupt a BIOS update, and keep the PC connected to power until it is finished.

fixes.title: When the hardware truly does not qualify, plan your next step
fixes.detail: Processors outside Microsoft's supported list cannot be made compliant with any setting. You can stay on Windows 10 (check Microsoft's published end-of-support date and the Extended Security Updates program) or move to supported hardware. A documented registry workaround exists (HKLM\SYSTEM\Setup\MoSetup, DWORD 'AllowUpgradesWithUnsupportedTPMOrCPU' = 1), but Microsoft says devices upgraded that way are not entitled to updates, so use it only as a last resort.
fixes.riskNote: Unsupported installations might not get updates, security fixes included, and could lose them at any point.

prevention: Turn on PTT or fTPM, UEFI mode and Secure Boot when building a new PC or doing a clean install
Check the PC with the PC Health Check app before planning a Windows 11 upgrade
Use GPT and UEFI for the system disk on every new Windows installation

title: "Windows can't verify the publisher of this driver software"
codes: Windows can't verify the publisher of this driver
Windows can't verify the publisher of this driver software
can't verify the publisher of this driver
summary: Partway through a driver install, Windows displays "Windows can't verify the publisher of this driver software." The package is not signed by a publisher Windows trusts, so it wants you to decide deliberately whether to install it anyway.
meaning: Windows confirms who published a driver by checking its digital certificate. You see this security warning for unsigned drivers, self-signed builds, and packages whose certificates have expired or been revoked. It is a checkpoint rather than a fault, and the question that matters is whether the driver really comes from the hardware vendor. Keep in mind that 64-bit Windows refuses to load unsigned kernel-mode drivers entirely, which shows up as a separate and stricter signature error.
commonCauses: The driver was downloaded from an unofficial mirror that repackaged it
The driver is truly unsigned, or a test or beta build that never went through WHQL signing
An old driver whose publisher certificate has expired or was revoked
Older hardware for which the vendor never released a signed driver for current Windows

fixes.title: Download the driver again from the official vendor site
fixes.detail: Get the package from the support page of your PC or device manufacturer, for your exact model. Unofficial driver download sites often repackage installers and strip or fake the signatures. A clean download from the official source resolves the warning the right way.

fixes.title: Check the digital signature before you decide
fixes.detail: Right-click the driver's .inf or .exe file and open Properties → Digital Signatures. Select the signature and click Details: you should see the signer's name and 'This digital signature is OK'. If a package that claims to be official has a missing or invalid signature, do not install it.

fixes.title: Allow the install only once the publisher checks out
fixes.detail: When both the vendor and the signature look right, go ahead and click 'Install this driver software anyway' in the warning dialog. If anything about the publisher seems off, cancel and look for a signed replacement driver instead.
fixes.riskNote: An unverified driver can run malicious or unstable code with high privileges. This override is meant for publishers you have verified, not as an everyday shortcut.

fixes.title: Find unsigned drivers with sigverif
fixes.detail: Press Win+R, type `sigverif` and click Start. The File Signature Verification tool lists the drivers on the system and marks unsigned files, which helps you spot the culprit if this warning keeps appearing for several devices.

fixes.title: Use a WHQL-signed or newer version
fixes.detail: See whether the vendor offers a newer, signed release of the driver. For very old hardware that has no signed driver for your version of Windows, try the generic class driver built into Windows: it is signed and usually handles the basic functions well enough.

prevention: Only download drivers from the hardware maker's official website
Choose WHQL-signed drivers over beta or modified builds
Avoid third-party 'driver updater' tools that install unsigned packages

title: Activation error 0xC004F012 (problem with the Software Licensing store)
summary: Activation fails with 0xC004F012. This Software Licensing Service error usually indicates that the local license store or token data is damaged, so Windows cannot read or report its own activation status.
meaning: The Software Licensing Service (sppsvc) is responsible for activation tokens and the local license store, and 0xC004F012 originates there. If that data gets corrupted, for example by a failed update, disk errors, or overly aggressive 'cleanup' tools, the service can no longer validate the license on the machine. Activation then fails even when the product key or digital license is completely valid.
commonCauses: The Software Licensing token store was corrupted by a failed update or a disk error
The Software Licensing Service (sppsvc) cannot start or has hung
Registry or system 'cleanup' tools removed licensing data
File system corruption on the system drive

fixes.title: Run the Activation troubleshooter
fixes.detail: Open Settings → System → Activation and select Troubleshoot. It checks again for a digital license tied to your Microsoft account and can bring activation back without any manual work on the license store.

fixes.title: Repair system files with DISM and SFC
fixes.detail: In a Command Prompt opened as administrator, run `DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth` and then `sfc /scannow`. This repairs damaged system files around the licensing components. Restart and try activating again.

fixes.title: Restart the licensing service and activate again
fixes.detail: From an elevated Command Prompt, run `net stop sppsvc`, then `net start sppsvc`, and then start activation with `slmgr /ato`. A stuck Software Licensing Service often recovers with nothing more than a clean restart.

fixes.title: Rebuild the license token store
fixes.detail: In an elevated Command Prompt, run `net stop sppsvc`. Rename `C:\Windows\System32\spp\store\2.0\tokens.dat` to `tokens.old` (from inside that folder, `ren tokens.dat tokens.old`). Then run `net start sppsvc` followed by `slmgr /ato`. Windows creates a new store and downloads the license again.
fixes.riskNote: Rename only tokens.dat and never delete the folder. On some systems the active store lives in C:\Windows\ServiceProfiles\NetworkService\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\SoftwareProtectionPlatform instead, so if you are unsure, stick with the troubleshooter.

fixes.title: Enter the key again or activate by phone
fixes.detail: Press Win+R and run `slui 3` to type in your product key, or `slui 4` to use the documented phone activation option if online activation still fails after repairing the store.

prevention: Link your Windows digital license to a Microsoft account (Settings → Activation)
Avoid registry and cleanup utilities that modify Software Protection data
Run `chkdsk` after power failures or crashes, since disk errors can corrupt the license store

title: Activation error 0xC004F034 (no license found, or the license is invalid)
summary: Activation fails with 0xC004F034. The Software Licensing Service either cannot locate a license that fits this device and Windows edition, or the one it locates is not valid for this installation.
meaning: 0xC004F034 is one of the Software Licensing activation errors. The service got as far as looking for a usable license and found nothing suitable for the device. This usually happens after hardware changes that no longer match the digital license's hardware fingerprint, after a clean install of an edition other than the one the license covers, or when the PC cannot contact Microsoft's activation servers to validate its license.
commonCauses: After replacing the motherboard or another major component, the digital license no longer matches the hardware fingerprint
The edition installed is not the edition the license is for
The key or license does not fit the installation channel (for example, a volume key on a retail install)
The PC is offline, or the network blocks Microsoft's activation endpoints

fixes.title: Sign in with the Microsoft account that holds the digital license
fixes.detail: Go to Settings → Accounts and sign in with the account you used on the earlier, activated installation, then look at Settings → System → Activation again. A linked digital license reactivates automatically once the hardware hash is a close enough match.

fixes.title: Run the Activation troubleshooter and use the hardware change option
fixes.detail: Open Settings → System → Activation → Troubleshoot. If the PC was recently rebuilt or had parts replaced, choose 'I changed hardware on this device recently', sign in, and link the license to this PC again.

fixes.title: Make sure the PC can reach the activation servers
fixes.detail: Check that websites load normally in a browser. Corporate networks, filtering proxies, or 'privacy' entries in the hosts file can all block activation. Try a different connection, such as a phone hotspot, and activate again.

fixes.title: Confirm your installed edition matches the license
fixes.detail: Look under Settings → System → About → 'Windows edition'. A Home license will not activate Pro, and a Pro license will not activate Home. Install the matching edition, or change the product key with `slui 3`.

fixes.title: Enter a valid key or activate by phone
fixes.detail: Press Win+R and run `slui 3` to type in a purchased key, or `slui 4` to reach the automated phone activation line. It checks the license on Microsoft's side and can handle cases that online activation cannot.

prevention: Link your digital license to a Microsoft account before changing any hardware
Write down your license type (retail or OEM) and edition before replacing components
Hold on to your proof of purchase for support and reactivation requests

title: 0x80070091: ERROR_DIR_NOT_EMPTY (The directory is not empty)
summary: You try to delete, rename or move a folder that looks empty, and Windows says "The directory is not empty" (0x80070091). Something inside it is either invisible to you or held open in a way Windows cannot easily release.
meaning: 0x80070091 corresponds to Win32 error 145, ERROR_DIR_NOT_EMPTY. While deleting, Windows found entries in the folder that it was unable to remove, such as hidden or system files, files that a program still has open, or entries whose records on disk are damaged. Usually this is a stuck state, not lost data. If the same folder fails again and again, though, that suggests file system corruption that deserves a check.
commonCauses: Hidden or system files (or reparse points) in the folder that Explorer does not display
A program, such as Explorer's preview pane, antivirus or a sync client, has files in the folder open
Leftover placeholder state from OneDrive or another sync or backup tool
A damaged directory index or records on the disk

fixes.title: Close whatever is using the folder and restart Explorer
fixes.detail: Close any programs and Explorer windows that are showing the folder. In Task Manager, right-click 'Windows Explorer' and choose Restart, then try deleting again. Open file handles are the most frequent cause.

fixes.title: Show hidden and system files
fixes.detail: In File Explorer, go to View → Show and turn on 'Hidden items'. Alternatively, in an elevated Command Prompt run `attrib -h -s "C:\path\to\folder\*.*" /s /d` to clear the hidden and system attributes within the folder so you can see what it actually contains.

fixes.title: Delete it from an elevated Command Prompt
fixes.detail: Start Command Prompt as administrator and run `rd /s /q "C:\path\to\folder"`. Deleting from the command line works in situations where Explorer gives up, stubborn reparse points included.
fixes.riskNote: `rd /s /q` removes the folder and everything in it permanently, and nothing lands in the Recycle Bin. Check the path carefully before you press Enter.

fixes.title: Pause sync and backup software
fixes.detail: Use the tray icon to pause OneDrive or any other sync or backup tool, then try the delete again. Placeholder files caught mid-sync cause exactly this error and are released when syncing stops.

fixes.title: Scan the disk for file system errors
fixes.detail: If the same folder fails every time, open an elevated Command Prompt and run `chkdsk C: /f` to fix damaged directory records. On the system drive, it will offer to run at the next restart.

prevention: Pause or close sync and backup clients before deleting large synced folders, rather than forcing the delete
Run `chkdsk` after improper shutdowns or when file errors keep recurring
Skip third-party 'unlocker' tools that install kernel hooks to force deletions

title: %1 is not a valid Win32 application (ERROR_BAD_EXE_FORMAT)
codes: %1 is not a valid Win32 application
summary: A program or installer will not start and Windows shows "%1 is not a valid Win32 application" (0x800700C1). The file is not an executable this system can run, most often because it was built for a different architecture or the download is corrupted or incomplete.
meaning: 0x800700C1 corresponds to Win32 error 193, ERROR_BAD_EXE_FORMAT. Windows only loads executables in a machine format it supports. 64-bit Windows on x86 hardware runs x64 programs and most x86 programs, but it cannot run ARM64 builds on Intel PCs, 16-bit legacy software, binaries for other operating systems such as Linux or macOS, or files that only look like executables because the download was cut short or damaged.
commonCauses: The wrong architecture was downloaded, such as an ARM64 build on 64-bit x86 Windows, or a mismatch the other way around
The download was truncated or corrupted, leaving an invalid executable
The file is a binary for another operating system, or an installer stub taken from the wrong package
A DLL or driver file is being run directly instead of being installed

fixes.title: Download the file again in full
fixes.detail: An incomplete or corrupted download is the most likely cause. Download it again on a reliable connection and, before running it, check the file size and any checksum the vendor publishes.

fixes.title: Get the build that fits your version of Windows
fixes.detail: Open Settings → System → About and look at 'System type' to see whether you have 64-bit x86 or an ARM-based PC. Then download the matching x64, x86 or ARM64 package from the vendor. Many download pages offer several builds side by side.

fixes.title: Make sure you are running the correct file
fixes.detail: Confirm it is the Windows installer and not the macOS or Linux version, and not an archive you need to extract first. Run the complete installer package instead of an .exe pulled out of it, since inner files can target a different platform.

fixes.title: Scan the file if its source is untrusted
fixes.detail: Malware is often distributed as corrupt or invalid executables that fail with this exact error. Right-click the file and choose 'Scan with Microsoft Defender', or run a custom scan from Windows Security → Virus & threat protection.

fixes.title: Developers: check the target platform
fixes.detail: If you compiled or published the program, verify the platform target (x86, x64 or ARM64) of the output binary, and confirm that every DLL you load matches the bitness of your process. A 64-bit process cannot load a 32-bit DLL, and a 32-bit process cannot load a 64-bit one.

prevention: Get installers only from official vendor sources
Compare file sizes and checksums against the published values before running unfamiliar downloads
Keep the full installer packages instead of executables extracted from them
